q: Large-core stroke trials (SELECT2, ANGEL-ASPECT) supported thrombectomy in anterior circulation LVO with an ASPECTS of:
e: These trials extended EVT to large-core infarcts (ASPECTS 3-5), with better functional outcomes than medical management.
p: ASPECTS: 10-point non-contrast CT score of the MCA territory; subtract 1 for each region with early ischaemic change. Regions: caudate, lentiform, internal capsule, insula, M1-M6 (basal ganglia and supraganglionic levels). Lower score = larger core. Older practice used 6 or more as the cutoff.

q: Which is NOT part of the Spetzler-Martin AVM grade?
e: The grade uses size, eloquence and venous drainage only.
p: Size: under 3 cm = 1, 3-6 cm = 2, over 6 cm = 3. Eloquent location = 1. Deep venous drainage = 1. Total gives grade I-V. I-II usually surgery, III multimodal, IV-V usually observation. Lawton supplementary score adds age, haemorrhagic presentation and diffuse nidus.

q: The most common site of hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage is the:
e: Putamen (about half), then thalamus, pons and cerebellum.
p: Deep (putaminal, thalamic, pontine, cerebellar) bleeds suggest hypertensive vasculopathy. Lobar bleeds in older patients suggest cerebral amyloid angiopathy (microbleeds and superficial siderosis on SWI, Boston criteria); in younger patients think AVM, tumour or venous thrombosis.

q: Which cystic brain lesion typically shows restricted diffusion in its central cavity?
e: Pus is viscous and hypercellular, so the abscess cavity is DWI bright with low ADC. Necrotic tumours usually facilitate.
p: Abscess: smooth thin T2-hypointense rim, thinner on the ventricular side, dual rim sign on SWI. Other restricted diffusion lesions: acute infarct, epidermoid, lymphoma, CJD, hyperviscosity. Arachnoid cyst follows CSF and suppresses on FLAIR.

q: The ideal common femoral artery puncture site is over the:
e: The mid-to-lower femoral head gives a compressible, safe common femoral stick.
p: Use fluoroscopy to find the femoral head, not the skin crease. High stick (above the inguinal ligament): retroperitoneal haematoma. Low stick (at or below the bifurcation): pseudoaneurysm, AV fistula, difficult compression. Ultrasound guidance reduces complications.
r: SIR access guidance; Kandarpa, Handbook of IR

q: A 6 Fr catheter has an outer diameter of about:
e: 1 Fr = 0.33 mm, so 6 Fr is about 2 mm.
p: Catheters are sized by OUTER diameter in French; sheaths by INNER diameter, so a 6 Fr sheath accepts a 6 Fr catheter. Wires are sized in inches (0.035, 0.018 and so on).

q: Which embolic agent is temporary, being resorbed over days to weeks?
e: Gelatin sponge (Gelfoam) is absorbed over days to weeks.
p: Temporary: gelatin sponge. Permanent: particles (PVA, microspheres), coils and plugs (mechanical, proximal occlusion), liquids (n-BCA glue, Onyx). Onyx is an EVOH copolymer in DMSO: non-adhesive, so it can be injected slowly into AVM nidi. n-BCA polymerises on contact with blood.

q: Per ACR guidance, metformin is withheld around iodinated contrast in patients with:
e: Withhold only with AKI or eGFR under 30, or intra-arterial contrast with likely first-pass renal exposure in impaired renal function.
p: Patients with eGFR 30 or more and no AKI need not stop it. When held, restart after about 48 hours if renal function is stable.

q: First-line drug for an anaphylactoid contrast reaction with hypotension and bronchospasm is:
e: Epinephrine is first line; steroids and antihistamines are adjuncts only.
p: Adult dose: 0.3 mg IM (0.3 mL of 1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh, repeat as needed. Atropine is for vagal reactions: bradycardia with hypotension. Anaphylaxis gives tachycardia.

q: Fleischner 2017: a single solid nodule under 6 mm in a low-risk patient needs:
e: Under 6 mm and low risk: no routine follow-up.
p: 6-8 mm: CT at 6-12 months, then consider 18-24 months. Over 8 mm: CT at 3 months, PET-CT or tissue sampling. High-risk patients under 6 mm: optional CT at 12 months. Not for age under 35, known cancer or immunosuppression.

q: In a cirrhotic liver, a 2 cm observation with arterial phase hyperenhancement and non-peripheral washout is LI-RADS:
e: APHE with 20 mm or more plus one additional major feature is LR-5.
p: LR-5 = definitely HCC. Major features: APHE, non-peripheral washout, enhancing capsule, threshold growth. LR-M = probably malignant but not HCC-specific, for example rim APHE or targetoid appearance.

q: Which examination gives the highest typical effective dose?
e: CT abdomen and pelvis is about 8-10 mSv.
p: Approximate effective doses: chest X-ray 0.02 mSv, mammogram 0.4, lumbar spine 1.5, CT head 2, CT chest 7, CT abdomen-pelvis 8-10. Natural background is about 3 mSv per year. Most diagnostic examinations give a fetal dose far below the 50 mGy deterministic threshold. ALARA applies.

q: The most common site of a ruptured saccular intracranial aneurysm is the:
e: The anterior communicating artery complex is the most common site, followed by the PCom and MCA bifurcation.
p: CT is positive in over 95% within 6 hours; CTA is the first-line vascular study and DSA the gold standard. Modified Fisher grade predicts vasospasm, which peaks at days 4-14. Perimesencephalic SAH is usually venous with a benign course.

q: The empty delta sign on contrast CT indicates thrombosis of the:
e: Non-enhancing clot within an enhancing sinus wall gives the empty delta sign in the posterior superior sagittal sinus.
p: Non-contrast signs: dense triangle (sinus) and cord sign (cortical vein). Confirm with CT or MR venography. Venous infarcts cross arterial territories and are often haemorrhagic. The transverse sinus is the most common site overall, then the superior sagittal sinus.

q: A hyperdense midline posterior fossa mass in a child with restricted diffusion is most likely:
e: Medulloblastoma is hypercellular, so it is hyperdense on CT with low ADC, and arises from the vermis.
p: Pilocytic astrocytoma: cerebellar hemisphere cyst with enhancing mural nodule, high ADC. Ependymoma: fourth ventricle floor, squeezes out through the foramina of Luschka and Magendie (plastic tumour), calcifies. Image the whole spine for CSF drop metastases.

q: In NASCET carotid stenosis measurement, the denominator is the diameter of the:
o: Normal distal ICA beyond the bulb
e: NASCET compares the narrowest lumen with the normal distal ICA; ECST estimates the original bulb diameter.
p: Percent stenosis = (1 - narrowest / distal normal ICA) x 100. Doppler consensus: PSV 125 cm/s or more suggests 50% or more, 230 cm/s or more suggests 70% or more. Symptomatic 70-99% stenosis has the strongest benefit from revascularisation.

q: The reversal agent for unfractionated heparin is:
e: Protamine neutralises heparin.
p: Rule of thumb: about 1 mg protamine per 100 units of heparin given in the last 2-3 hours, maximum 50 mg, given slowly. Risks: hypotension and anaphylaxis (NPH insulin users, fish allergy, prior vasectomy). Vitamin K reverses warfarin, idarucizumab dabigatran, andexanet factor Xa inhibitors.

q: Which Doppler finding is characteristic of a femoral artery pseudoaneurysm?
e: Flow into the sac in systole and back out in diastole gives a to-and-fro waveform in the neck.
p: Colour Doppler shows the yin-yang sign in the sac. Treatment: US-guided thrombin injection (preferred), compression for small ones, surgery if large, infected or skin compromise. A femoral AV fistula instead shows turbulent flow with an arterialised venous waveform.

q: For a high bleeding-risk IR procedure (SIR 2019), platelets should be above about:
e: High-risk procedures need platelets above about 50,000/uL and INR corrected to about 1.5-1.8.
p: Low-risk (venous access, paracentesis, thoracentesis, dialysis access): INR up to 2-3, platelets above about 20,000/uL. High-risk (solid organ and deep biopsy, biliary intervention, TIPS): stricter limits. Thresholds are guideline-based, so always check local protocol.

q: Which HRCT finding is typical of a UIP pattern?
e: UIP is basal and subpleural, with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis.
p: 2018 categories: UIP, probable UIP, indeterminate, alternative diagnosis. Features pointing away from UIP: upper or mid zone predominance, peribronchovascular pattern, extensive ground glass, profuse micronodules, cysts, mosaic attenuation with air-trapping (think fibrotic HP, sarcoid).

q: The primary lung cancer most likely to cavitate is:
e: Squamous cell carcinoma cavitates most often.
p: Cavity wall thickness: 4 mm or less usually benign, over 15 mm usually malignant. Adenocarcinoma is the most common type overall and is peripheral. Small cell is central with bulky hilar and mediastinal nodes. Carcinoid is endobronchial.
r: Fraser and Pare; Radiographics lung cancer review

q: The most common functioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour is:
e: Insulinoma is the most common functioning pNET.
p: Insulinoma: usually under 2 cm, solitary, mostly benign, hypervascular on arterial phase. Gastrinoma: gastrinoma triangle (duodenum and pancreatic head), often malignant, linked with MEN1 and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. Non-functioning tumours are the commonest overall.

q: The upper limit of normal appendix diameter on graded-compression ultrasound is:
e: An appendix over 6 mm that is non-compressible suggests appendicitis.
p: Supporting signs: wall thickening, appendicolith, hyperechoic periappendiceal fat, local fluid, hyperaemia. In children and pregnancy use US first, then MRI if equivocal. A non-visualised appendix with no secondary signs makes appendicitis unlikely.

q: Which Bosniak category carries about a 50% risk of malignancy and usually prompts surgical consideration?
e: Category III is indeterminate, with thickened enhancing walls or septa, and about half are malignant.
p: I and II: benign, no follow-up. IIF: follow-up imaging. III: about 50% malignant. IV: about 90%, with enhancing soft-tissue components. The 2019 update adds MRI and defines septa and wall thickness more precisely.

q: A lipid-rich adrenal adenoma is diagnosed on unenhanced CT when attenuation is:
e: Attenuation of 10 HU or less reflects intracellular fat.
p: If above 10 HU: washout CT, absolute washout 60% or more and relative washout 40% or more at 15 minutes favour adenoma. Opposed-phase MRI shows signal drop. Phaeochromocytoma enhances avidly and can be very bright on T2.

q: Which periosteal reaction suggests an aggressive lesion?
e: Codman triangle, sunburst and lamellated (onion skin) reactions all indicate rapid growth.
p: Benign patterns: solid, thick, wavy or smooth. Onion skin is classic for Ewing sarcoma, sunburst for osteosarcoma. Also assess the zone of transition (narrow is benign, wide is aggressive), cortical destruction and soft-tissue mass.

q: A Segond fracture is strongly associated with injury to the:
e: Segond fracture is a lateral tibial plateau avulsion and almost always accompanies an ACL tear.
p: Other ACL signs: pivot-shift bone bruise (lateral femoral condyle and posterolateral tibia), deep lateral femoral notch, anterior tibial translation, empty notch sign. O'Donoghue triad: ACL, MCL and medial meniscus.

q: The most common source of haemorrhage in pelvic fractures is:
e: Most pelvic bleeding is venous or from cancellous bone; arterial bleeding is the minority.
p: Arterial bleeding (about 10-15%; superior gluteal and internal pudendal branches) shows as a contrast blush on CT and is treated by angioembolisation. Binder, preperitoneal packing and external fixation control venous bleeding. Young-Burgess classifies by force vector.
r: EAST and WSES pelvic trauma guidelines

q: The most common type of paediatric intussusception is:
e: Ileocolic intussusception accounts for the great majority.
p: Typical age 3 months to 3 years, with a pathological lead point (Meckel, polyp, lymphoma) more likely in older children. US shows a target (doughnut) sign. Air or hydrostatic reduction is first line; peritonitis or perforation contraindicates it.

q: BI-RADS 3 carries a probability of malignancy of:
e: BI-RADS 3 (probably benign) is 2% or less, managed with short-interval follow-up.
p: 4A: over 2% to 10%. 4B: over 10% to 50%. 4C: over 50% to under 95%. 5: 95% or more. 0: incomplete. 6: known biopsy-proven. Classic category 3 findings: non-calcified circumscribed solid mass, focal asymmetry, grouped punctate calcifications.

q: The nuchal translucency scan is performed between:
e: NT is measured at 11 to 13+6 weeks, with CRL 45-84 mm.
p: Increased NT (commonly 3.5 mm or more) raises risk of aneuploidy (trisomy 21), cardiac defects and genetic syndromes. Combined screening adds free beta-hCG and PAPP-A. Nasal bone and ductus venosus flow refine risk.

q: Posterior acoustic enhancement on ultrasound is seen behind:
e: Fluid attenuates less than surrounding tissue, so structures behind it appear brighter.
p: Acoustic shadowing: calculi, bone, dense calcification; dirty shadowing: gas. Comet-tail or ring-down: gas bubbles and metal. Also know reverberation, mirror image, edge shadowing and side-lobe artefacts.

q: DAWN extended thrombectomy eligibility (clinical-core mismatch) up to how long after last known well?
e: DAWN selected patients 6-24 hours from last known well using clinical-core mismatch.
p: DEFUSE-3: 6-16 hours with perfusion mismatch (core under 70 mL, mismatch ratio 1.8 or more, mismatch volume 15 mL or more). Standard IV thrombolysis window is 4.5 hours. Perfusion software such as RAPID helps select late-window patients.

q: Which is NOT one of the McDonald 2017 topographies for dissemination in space in MS?
e: The four areas are periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial and spinal cord.
p: DIS: one or more T2 lesions in at least 2 of the 4 areas. DIT: new T2 or enhancing lesion on follow-up, simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions, or CSF oligoclonal bands (2017). MS spinal lesions are short (under 2 segments); NMOSD gives longitudinally extensive lesions (3 or more segments).

q: A butterfly lesion crossing the corpus callosum is most typical of:
e: Glioblastoma spreads along white-matter tracts across the corpus callosum.
p: GBM: ring enhancement, necrotic centre, perilesional oedema, raised rCBV. Lymphoma can also cross the callosum but enhances homogeneously with restricted diffusion. Abscess has a smooth rim and restricted centre. Note WHO 2021: glioblastoma is IDH-wildtype.

q: The most common intramedullary spinal cord tumour in adults is:
e: Ependymoma is the commonest in adults; astrocytoma is the commonest in children.
p: Ependymoma: central, symmetric, cap sign (haemosiderin), associated with NF2. Myxopapillary type arises at the conus or filum. Astrocytoma: eccentric. Haemangioblastoma: cyst with enhancing nodule and flow voids, think VHL.
r: Osborn's Brain; Radiographics spinal cord tumours

q: On dynamic contrast MRI, a pituitary microadenoma typically appears:
o: Hypoenhancing relative to the normal gland early on
Isointense to the gland at all phases
e: The normal gland enhances avidly and early; a microadenoma enhances more slowly.
p: Microadenoma is under 10 mm and macroadenoma 10 mm or more. Macroadenoma may give a snowman appearance at the diaphragma sellae. Apoplexy shows haemorrhage. Differentials: Rathke cleft cyst, craniopharyngioma.

q: Which guidewire is best suited to crossing a tortuous, tight stenosis?
e: Hydrophilic wires are slippery and steerable, but carry higher risk of subintimal passage and perforation.
p: Bentson: floppy tip, atraumatic for access. Amplatz Super Stiff: support for stent grafts and exchanges. Never advance a wire against resistance, always keep the tip in view, keep hydrophilic wires wet, and never pull a wire back through a needle (shearing).

q: The best-supported indication for an IVC filter is acute proximal DVT or PE with:
e: Filters are for those who cannot be anticoagulated, or who fail anticoagulation.
p: Retrievable filters should be removed once the contraindication resolves. Do a cavogram first to check anatomy (duplicated IVC, left-sided IVC, retroaortic renal vein) and IVC diameter (megacava over about 28-30 mm limits standard filters). Complications: migration, IVC thrombosis, fracture, perforation.
r: SIR IVC filter guidelines; CHEST guidelines

q: A standard TIPS typically connects the:
o: Right hepatic vein to right portal vein
Left hepatic vein to left portal vein
Middle hepatic vein to splenic vein
e: The usual tract runs from the right hepatic vein to the right portal vein.
p: Indications: refractory variceal bleeding, refractory ascites; pre-emptive TIPS in high-risk bleeders. Contraindications: heart failure, severe pulmonary hypertension, polycystic liver, uncontrolled encephalopathy, biliary obstruction. Covered stents improve patency. Aim for a portosystemic gradient under 12 mmHg. Main complication: hepatic encephalopathy.

q: On CTPA, an RV:LV diameter ratio above which value suggests right heart strain?
e: A ratio above 1.0 suggests RV strain.
p: Other signs: septal bowing toward the LV, contrast reflux into the IVC and hepatic veins, dilated main PA (over about 29 mm). Parenchymal signs: Hampton hump (peripheral wedge opacity), Westermark sign (focal oligaemia). Fleischner sign is an enlarged central pulmonary artery.

q: The tree-in-bud pattern on CT most commonly indicates:
e: Tree-in-bud reflects impaction of small airways with mucus, pus or debris.
p: Causes: endobronchial TB, MAC, bacterial pneumonia, aspiration, cystic fibrosis, bronchiolitis. Perilymphatic nodules (sarcoid, silicosis) follow septa and fissures. Random nodules suggest miliary TB or metastases. Centrilobular nodules spare the pleura.

q: The typical enhancement pattern of a hepatic haemangioma is:
o: Peripheral nodular discontinuous enhancement with centripetal fill-in
Rim arterial enhancement with central scar
e: Discontinuous peripheral nodules enlarge and fill in toward the centre, following blood pool.
p: Very bright on T2 (light-bulb sign). Giant haemangiomas may keep a non-enhancing central scar. FNH: central scar, spoke-wheel arterial enhancement, near-isointense in other phases. Adenoma: arterial enhancement, fat, haemorrhage.

q: The best time for CECT to assess pancreatic necrosis in acute pancreatitis is:
e: Necrosis is best defined from about 72 hours after onset.
p: Early CT underestimates necrosis. Early imaging is for diagnostic doubt or deterioration. Revised Atlanta: interstitial oedematous vs necrotising pancreatitis; collections within 4 weeks are acute (peripancreatic fluid, acute necrotic collection); after 4 weeks they become pseudocyst or walled-off necrosis.

q: The dominant sequence for transition zone lesions in PI-RADS v2.1 is:
e: T2W dominates for transition zone; DWI dominates for the peripheral zone.
p: Scores run 1-5; 4 means clinically significant cancer is likely and 5 very likely. In the PZ, DCE only upgrades a DWI score of 3 to 4. Classic TZ cancer: erased charcoal sign on T2.

q: The double-line sign on T2 MRI is characteristic of:
e: A band-like double line separates necrotic from viable bone in AVN.
p: Radiograph clue: subchondral crescent sign. ARCO staging guides management. Transient marrow oedema lacks the band-like line and resolves. Causes of AVN: steroids, alcohol, sickle cell disease, trauma.
r: Resnick, Bone and Joint Imaging; ARCO

q: The small bowel faeces sign suggests:
o: Mechanical small bowel obstruction near the transition point
e: Faeces-like content in dilated small bowel is seen proximal to the transition point.
p: Adhesions are the commonest cause of SBO. Signs of strangulation: reduced wall enhancement, mesenteric swirl, closed loop (C-shaped, radially arranged), free fluid. Ileus: diffuse dilatation including colon without a transition point.

q: A neonate with double bubble sign and no distal bowel gas most likely has:
e: Double bubble with absent distal gas indicates complete duodenal obstruction.
p: About 30% of cases are associated with Down syndrome. Midgut volvulus: UGI shows the duodenojejunal flexure not to the left of the spine, corkscrew duodenum, SMV rotation around SMA. Pyloric stenosis: muscle thickness 3 mm or more and channel length about 15 mm or more.

q: Fine pleomorphic or fine linear branching calcifications most suggest:
e: Fine pleomorphic and fine linear morphologies carry the highest malignancy risk.
p: Suspicious morphology: amorphous, coarse heterogeneous, fine pleomorphic, fine linear or branching. Distribution: grouped, linear, segmental (linear and segmental are more worrying). Typically benign: skin, vascular, popcorn, rod-like, round, rim, milk of calcium, dystrophic.

q: Which ultrasound feature is most suggestive of malignancy?
e: A taller-than-wide, non-parallel orientation suggests malignancy.
p: Other suspicious features: irregular shape, spiculated or angular margins, hypoechoic mass, posterior shadowing, calcifications, architectural distortion. Benign leaning: oval, parallel, circumscribed. Elastography often shows stiffness in cancer.

q: In ACR MRI safety zoning, the magnet room is:
e: Zone IV is the scanner room itself.
p: Zone I: public. Zone II: reception and screening. Zone III: restricted access to screened personnel only; unscreened entry is dangerous. Zone IV: magnet room, always under supervision. Check implants for MR conditional status; a quench vents helium.

q: An Agatston coronary calcium score generally indicating severe plaque burden is:
e: 400 or more is usually classed as severe.
p: A score of 0 means very low short-term risk. Bands vary by source: 1-99 mild, 100-399 moderate, 400 or more severe (some use 1-10 minimal). CAD-RADS: 0 none, 1 under 25% stenosis, 2 25-49%, 3 50-69%, 4A 70-99%, 4B left main over 50% or three-vessel 70% or more, 5 total occlusion.

q: An epidural haematoma is typically limited by the:
o: Nothing; it crosses all of these
e: Epidural blood strips the dura off the skull until it meets a suture.
p: Biconvex (lentiform), from a middle meningeal artery tear with temporal bone fracture; swirl sign suggests active bleeding. Subdural: crescentic, crosses sutures, stopped by falx and tentorium, from bridging veins.

q: T2/FLAIR hyperintensity of mammillary bodies, medial thalami and periaqueductal grey matter in an alcoholic patient suggests:
e: This is the classic distribution of thiamine deficiency.
p: Mammillary bodies may enhance. Osmotic demyelination: central pontine T2 hyperintensity with sparing of the periphery. HSV: asymmetric medial temporal, insular and cingulate disease. CJD: cortical ribboning and basal ganglia on DWI.

q: PRES most commonly affects the:
e: Posterior parieto-occipital subcortical vasogenic oedema is typical.
p: Triggers: hypertension, eclampsia, tacrolimus, cyclosporine. High ADC (vasogenic). Haemorrhage and enhancement can occur; atypical sites include frontal, cerebellar and brainstem. Usually reversible with treatment of the cause.

q: Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma in tuberous sclerosis arises near the:
e: SEGA grows at the foramen of Monro and can cause hydrocephalus.
p: Subependymal nodules (candle guttering) calcify; a nodule that grows and enhances, over about 1 cm, is SEGA. Other findings: cortical tubers, renal angiomyolipomas, cardiac rhabdomyomas, lung LAM.

q: Moyamoya disease features progressive stenosis of the:
e: Terminal ICA stenosis with basal collaterals gives the puff of smoke angiographic appearance.
p: FLAIR ivy sign reflects slow leptomeningeal flow. Children present with ischaemia, adults often with haemorrhage. Six Suzuki stages. Treatment is revascularisation (for example STA-MCA bypass). Moyamoya syndrome: NF1, sickle cell, Down syndrome, prior radiation.

q: A haematoma that is T1 hyperintense and T2 hypointense most likely contains:
e: Early subacute blood (about 3-7 days) has intracellular methaemoglobin.
p: Hyperacute (under 24 h): T1 iso, T2 bright (oxyHb). Acute (1-3 days): T1 iso, T2 dark (deoxyHb). Early subacute: T1 bright, T2 dark. Late subacute (over 7 days): T1 and T2 bright (extracellular metHb). Chronic: dark haemosiderin rim.

q: Minimum future liver remnant usually required before resection in a normal liver is about:
e: About 20% in a healthy liver.
p: Needs rise to about 30% after chemotherapy or with steatosis, and 40% in cirrhosis. Portal vein embolisation (usually right PVE) induces contralateral hypertrophy over about 2-6 weeks. ALPPS is an alternative.

q: The most common indication for uterine artery embolisation is:
e: Symptomatic leiomyomata, mainly heavy bleeding and bulk symptoms.
p: Bilateral embolisation with particles of about 500-900 microns. Complications: post-embolisation syndrome, infection, premature ovarian failure. Contraindications: pregnancy, active infection, suspected gynaecological malignancy. Also used for postpartum haemorrhage.

q: TACE is the recommended first-line treatment for HCC in BCLC stage:
e: Intermediate (stage B) multinodular HCC with preserved liver function.
p: BCLC 0/A: resection, ablation or transplant. C: systemic therapy (for example atezolizumab with bevacizumab). D: best supportive care. TACE needs a patent portal vein and adequate liver function (Child-Pugh A or B7).

q: The approximate skin dose threshold for transient erythema is:
e: About 2 Gy; skin effects are deterministic.
p: Temporary epilation starts at about 3 Gy. Reduce dose: pulsed low-rate fluoroscopy, collimation, minimal magnification, image receptor close to the patient, tube far from the patient, avoid steep angles, vary the beam entry point. Track air kerma and DAP.

q: The deep sulcus sign on a supine chest radiograph indicates:
e: Air collects anteromedially in the supine position, deepening the costophrenic sulcus.
p: Tension signs: mediastinal shift, flattened or inverted hemidiaphragm. CT is the most sensitive test. A skin fold can mimic a pneumothorax line.

q: Pulmonary sequestration receives its arterial supply from:
o: A systemic artery, usually the aorta
e: Sequestered lung has an anomalous systemic arterial supply and no normal bronchial connection.
p: Intralobar (more common, presents later, pulmonary venous drainage) versus extralobar (own pleura, systemic venous drainage, associated anomalies, younger). Usual site: posterior basal left lower lobe.

q: Subcarinal lymph nodes are IASLC station:
e: Station 7 is subcarinal.
p: 4R: right lower paratracheal. 5: aortopulmonary window. 6: para-aortic. 8: paraoesophageal. 9: pulmonary ligament. 10: hilar. N2 means ipsilateral mediastinal or subcarinal; N3 means contralateral or supraclavicular. Short axis over 1 cm is abnormal.

q: The comb sign in Crohn disease reflects:
o: Engorged vasa recta next to inflamed bowel
e: Hypervascularity of the mesentery gives comb-like vessels perpendicular to the inflamed wall.
p: Other signs: creeping fat, mural stratification, skip lesions, cobblestoning. String sign of Kantor is terminal ileal narrowing on barium. MR enterography assesses activity without radiation.

q: In Budd-Chiari syndrome the caudate lobe is characteristically:
e: Caudate veins drain directly into the IVC, so the lobe is spared and hypertrophies.
p: Other findings: non-visualised or thrombosed hepatic veins, comma-shaped intrahepatic collaterals, patchy central enhancement, IVC narrowing. Cirrhosis can also enlarge the caudate with right lobe atrophy.

q: In IPMN, a main pancreatic duct of 10 mm or more is:
e: Main duct 10 mm or more is a high-risk stigma (Fukuoka 2017).
p: Worrisome: cyst 3 cm or more, thickened enhancing walls, MPD 5-9 mm, non-enhancing mural nodule, abrupt duct calibre change. Other high-risk: obstructive jaundice with a head cyst, enhancing mural nodule 5 mm or more. Branch-duct IPMN looks like a cluster of grapes.

q: Haemorrhage risk in renal angiomyolipoma increases above a size of about:
e: Lesions over about 4 cm, and aneurysms over about 5 mm, carry a higher bleeding risk.
p: Diagnosis rests on macroscopic fat (HU under -20). Multiple bilateral lesions suggest tuberous sclerosis. Presentation with spontaneous retroperitoneal bleeding is Wunderlich syndrome. Treatment: selective embolisation or mTOR inhibitors.

q: The imaging test of choice for suspected renal colic in a non-pregnant adult is:
e: Non-contrast CT is the most accurate for urolithiasis.
p: Indirect signs: hydronephrosis, perinephric stranding. Stones of 5 mm or less usually pass. Ultrasound is preferred in pregnancy and children. Uric acid stones are radiolucent on radiographs but visible on CT.

q: The nidus of an osteoid osteoma is typically no larger than:
e: The nidus is up to about 1.5 cm; larger is osteoblastoma.
p: Night pain relieved by NSAIDs. CT shows a lucent nidus with central calcification and reactive sclerosis. Treatment: percutaneous radiofrequency ablation or surgery.

q: The most commonly torn rotator cuff tendon is the:
e: Supraspinatus tears most often, usually near its critical zone.
p: Full-thickness tear: fluid-signal gap on T2 fat-saturated images. Subscapularis tear may accompany biceps tendon subluxation. Hooked type III acromion predisposes to impingement. Goutallier grades fatty atrophy.

q: Giant cell tumour of bone typically arises in the:
o: Epiphysis of a skeletally mature patient
Metaphysis of a child with a sclerotic rim
e: It is epiphyseal, abutting the subarticular surface, after physeal closure.
p: Eccentric lytic lesion, common at distal femur, proximal tibia and distal radius. Chondroblastoma is epiphyseal in skeletally immature patients. ABC shows fluid-fluid levels. Denosumab is used for unresectable disease.

q: A Stanford type A aortic dissection involves the:
e: Any dissection involving the ascending aorta is type A and usually needs emergency surgery.
p: Type B (distal to the left subclavian) is managed medically with blood pressure and heart rate control; TEVAR for malperfusion, rupture or refractory pain. Intramural haematoma shows a crescentic high-attenuation wall on unenhanced CT. Use ECG-gated CTA.

q: The most common site of ectopic pregnancy is the:
e: The ampulla accounts for the majority.
p: Free fluid in Morison pouch suggests rupture. Cornual pregnancy has a higher rupture risk. No intrauterine pregnancy above the hCG discriminatory zone (about 1500-3500 mIU/mL) is suspicious. Heterotopic pregnancy is uncommon.

q: Which feature favours neuroblastoma over Wilms tumour?
o: Tumour thrombus in the renal vein
Calcification with vascular encasement crossing the midline
e: Neuroblastoma is extrarenal, often calcified, and encases rather than displaces vessels.
p: Wilms: intrarenal, claw sign, displaces vessels, venous tumour thrombus, age 3-4. Neuroblastoma: adrenal or sympathetic chain origin, younger age, raised urine VMA and HVA, MIBG avid.

q: Klein line on an AP hip radiograph is used to diagnose:
e: A line along the superior femoral neck should intersect the femoral head; failure suggests SCFE.
p: Image with AP and frog-leg lateral views. Typical patient is an obese adolescent. DDH uses Hilgenreiner and Perkin lines and the acetabular index. Perthes is avascular necrosis at about 4-8 years.

q: BI-RADS breast density 'heterogeneously dense' is category:
e: Category C: heterogeneously dense, which may obscure small masses.
p: A: almost entirely fatty. B: scattered fibroglandular. D: extremely dense, lowering sensitivity. Density is a visual assessment. Supplemental screening options: ultrasound, MRI (including abbreviated), contrast-enhanced mammography. Tomosynthesis improves detection.

q: Which MRI kinetic curve type is most suspicious?
e: Rapid initial rise with washout in the delayed phase is type III.
p: Type II is intermediate. Kinetics supplement morphology; irregular spiculated margins and rim enhancement carry more weight. Low ADC on DWI supports malignancy. Silicone implant rupture shows the linguine sign.

q: The strongest risk factor for placenta accreta spectrum is:
o: Placenta previa with prior caesarean section
e: Previa over a uterine scar carries the highest risk.
p: Ultrasound signs: loss of retroplacental clear zone, placental lacunae, bladder wall interruption, subplacental hypervascularity. MRI assesses depth (accreta, increta, percreta). IR may place balloon occlusion catheters or perform uterine artery embolisation.

q: Doubling the mAs in CT will:
o: Reduce noise by about 30% and double dose
e: Noise falls with the square root of dose, so doubling mAs reduces noise by about 29%.
p: Dose scales linearly with mAs and roughly with kVp squared. Iterative reconstruction and automatic exposure control reduce dose. Higher pitch lowers dose per rotation but can degrade image quality.
r: Bushberg, Essential Physics of Medical Imaging

q: A superscan on bone scintigraphy suggests:
e: Intense, diffuse skeletal uptake with absent renal and bladder activity.
p: Prostate cancer is the classic cause; metabolic bone disease such as hyperparathyroidism can mimic it. Flare phenomenon is apparent progression soon after therapy. Photopenic lesions: myeloma, renal cell carcinoma.

q: Periarticular osteopenia with marginal erosions and uniform joint space loss suggests:
e: Symmetric small-joint disease with erosions, osteopenia and no bone production is typical of RA.
p: RA: MCP, PIP, ulnar styloid. OA: osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts, asymmetric loss. Gout: punched-out erosions with overhanging edges, tophi, preserved joint space. Psoriatic: DIP, pencil-in-cup, periostitis, sausage digit.

q: A scaphoid waist fracture most commonly complicates with:
o: Avascular necrosis of the proximal pole
Avascular necrosis of the distal pole
e: Blood supply enters distally, so the proximal pole is at risk.
p: First radiographs can be normal. If clinical suspicion persists, immobilise and repeat at 10-14 days or do MRI. Use dedicated scaphoid views (ulnar deviation). Non-union and carpal collapse (SNAC wrist) follow.

q: The fallen fragment sign is seen in a:
e: A pathological fracture through a simple cyst lets a cortical fragment fall to the dependent cyst floor.
p: Simple cyst: central metaphyseal lucency in a child, proximal humerus or femur, does not expand much. ABC: eccentric, expansile, fluid-fluid levels. Fibrous dysplasia: ground-glass matrix, shepherd crook deformity.

q: The double PCL sign on knee MRI suggests:
e: A displaced inner meniscal fragment lies in the notch beneath the PCL.
p: Also look for an absent bow-tie sign and a flipped fragment. Discoid meniscus: bow-tie seen on three or more contiguous sagittal slices. Medial tears are more common than lateral.

q: A markedly raised AFP in a testicular germ cell tumour suggests a component of:
e: AFP is produced by yolk sac elements; pure seminoma has normal AFP.
p: Pure seminoma may have mildly raised hCG. Choriocarcinoma: markedly raised hCG. Lymphoma is the commonest testicular tumour over 60. Nodal spread goes to the retroperitoneum first (right interaortocaval, left para-aortic).

q: The most common RCC subtype, typically hypervascular on the corticomedullary phase, is:
e: Clear cell RCC accounts for about 70-75%.
p: Papillary: hypovascular, often multifocal. Chromophobe: spoke-wheel enhancement, associated with Birt-Hogg-Dube. Clear cell links to VHL. T1a tumours (4 cm or less) can be treated with percutaneous ablation.

q: The most common ovarian germ cell tumour is:
e: Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid) is the commonest.
p: Features: fat-fluid level, Rokitansky nodule, tip of the iceberg sign on US, signal drop on fat suppression. Complications: torsion, rupture, rarely malignant change (squamous cell carcinoma).

q: The upper limit of normal gallbladder wall thickness on ultrasound is:
e: Over 3 mm is abnormal, though non-specific.
p: Acute cholecystitis: stones, sonographic Murphy sign, wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid. HIDA non-filling of the gallbladder supports it. Thick walls also occur with hepatitis, ascites and heart failure. Gas suggests emphysematous cholecystitis.

q: The most common type of choledochal cyst (Todani) is:
e: Type I, fusiform dilatation of the extrahepatic duct, is 80-90%.
p: II: diverticulum. III: choledochocele. IVa/b: multiple cysts. V: Caroli disease. Associated with anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction and a raised risk of cholangiocarcinoma.

q: A central scar that is T2 hypointense favours:
e: Fibrolamellar HCC has a fibrous, T2-dark scar; the FNH scar is T2-bright.
p: FNH: bright scar that enhances late, no capsule. Fibrolamellar: young non-cirrhotic patient, large mass, calcification, lymph nodes, normal AFP.

q: Calcified diaphragmatic pleural plaques indicate previous exposure to:
e: Plaques are the commonest asbestos-related finding.
p: Latency is 20 years or more. Plaques spare the costophrenic angles and apices. Rounded atelectasis gives a comet tail. Asbestosis: basal subpleural fibrosis. Mesothelioma: nodular pleural thickening, mediastinal pleural involvement.

q: Bilateral symmetric hilar nodes with right paratracheal nodes (1-2-3 sign) suggest:
e: The 1-2-3 sign (right paratracheal plus both hila) is classic for sarcoid.
p: Scadding stages: I hilar nodes, II nodes plus lung disease, III lung disease only, IV fibrosis. Perilymphatic nodules follow bronchovascular bundles and subpleural regions. Eggshell calcification also occurs in silicosis. TB is usually asymmetric.

q: Popcorn calcification with fat in a solitary pulmonary nodule suggests:
e: Fat (about -40 to -120 HU) plus popcorn calcification is diagnostic of hamartoma.
p: Benign calcification patterns: diffuse, central, laminated (granuloma) and popcorn (hamartoma). Eccentric or stippled calcification is worrisome.

q: The steeple sign on an AP neck radiograph indicates:
e: Subglottic narrowing gives the steeple sign in croup.
p: Epiglottitis: thumb sign and thick aryepiglottic folds on the lateral view. Retropharyngeal abscess: widened prevertebral soft tissue (about 7 mm at C2 and 14 mm at C6 in children).

q: Which finding is most specific for abusive injury in an infant?
e: Corner and bucket-handle metaphyseal lesions are highly specific.
p: Posterior rib fractures are also highly specific. Do a skeletal survey under 2 years, repeat at about 2 weeks. Subdural haemorrhages of differing ages and spiral femur fractures in non-ambulant infants raise concern.

q: The lemon and banana signs on fetal ultrasound indicate:
e: Frontal bone scalloping (lemon) and a wrapped cerebellum (banana) go with Chiari II and open spina bifida.
p: Often ventriculomegaly as well. Maternal serum AFP is raised. Folic acid prevents many cases. Prenatal repair was studied in the MOMS trial.

q: The most common coronary dominance pattern is:
e: About 70-85% are right dominant (PDA from the RCA).
p: The left main divides into LAD and LCx. An anomalous coronary with an interarterial course (between aorta and pulmonary trunk) is the high-risk variant for sudden death.

q: Diffusely increased uptake in a symmetrically enlarged thyroid on scintigraphy suggests:
e: Graves disease gives diffusely increased uptake.
p: Subacute thyroiditis: low uptake. Toxic adenoma: a single hot nodule with suppressed background gland. A cold nodule needs FNA, as a minority are malignant.

q: Rigler sign (gas on both sides of the bowel wall) indicates:
e: Gas on both sides outlines the bowel wall in pneumoperitoneum.
p: Erect chest radiograph is most sensitive for free gas (about 1 mL). Football sign: large pneumoperitoneum. Falciform ligament sign. Chilaiditi sign mimics free gas. CT is the most sensitive test.

q: Fat typically measures about what attenuation on CT?
e: Fat is about -100 HU.
p: Air -1000, water 0, acute blood about 50-70, soft tissue about 30-60, cortical bone high. Fat suppression on MRI relies on its short T1.
r: Bushberg, Essential Physics of Medical Imaging

q: The ophthalmic artery arises from the:
e: It arises just after the ICA exits the cavernous sinus.
p: PCom and anterior choroidal arise from the communicating segment. ECA-ophthalmic anastomoses (for example via the middle meningeal artery) matter in embolisation: non-target embolisation can cause blindness.

q: A Barrow type A carotid-cavernous fistula is:
o: A direct high-flow ICA to cavernous sinus shunt
A dural shunt fed by ECA branches only
A dural shunt fed by ICA branches only
A dural shunt fed by both ICA and ECA branches
e: Type A is direct and high-flow, usually from trauma or a ruptured cavernous aneurysm.
p: B: ICA dural branches. C: ECA dural branches. D: both. Pulsatile exophthalmos, chemosis, bruit and a dilated superior ophthalmic vein. Treatment: endovascular (transarterial or transvenous coils, balloon, liquid embolic).

q: The straight sinus is formed by the inferior sagittal sinus and the:
e: The vein of Galen joins the inferior sagittal sinus to form the straight sinus, draining to the torcula.
p: The vein of Galen is formed by the two internal cerebral veins and the basal veins. A vein of Galen malformation presents in neonates with high-output heart failure and is treated by staged transarterial embolisation.

q: Cervical ICA dissection typically begins:
o: About 2 cm beyond the bulb, sparing the bulb
At the origin from the CCA
e: It usually starts distal to the bulb and extends toward the petrous segment.
p: Flame-shaped tapering or string sign on angiography. T1 fat-sat MRI: crescent of hyperintense mural haematoma. Horner syndrome may occur. Associations: FMD, Ehlers-Danlos. Treatment is usually antithrombotic.

q: The most common aortic arch variant is:
o: Left vertebral artery from the arch
e: A common origin of the brachiocephalic and left common carotid arteries is seen in a sizeable minority.
p: Normal branching: brachiocephalic, left CCA, left subclavian. Left vertebral from the arch in about 5%. Aberrant right subclavian (arteria lusoria) is retroesophageal and uncommon. Arch variants change catheter choice for carotid and neuro intervention.

q: A string-of-beads renal artery in a young woman suggests:
e: Medial fibroplasia gives alternating stenoses and dilatations in the mid-distal artery.
p: Atherosclerotic stenosis is ostial and treated with stenting; FMD responds to balloon angioplasty, usually without a stent. PAN: microaneurysms. Takayasu: aortic wall thickening in young women. FMD also affects carotid arteries.

q: The most sensitive test for slow lower GI bleeding is:
e: Scintigraphy detects bleeds as slow as about 0.1-0.2 mL/min.
p: CTA detects about 0.3-0.5 mL/min, catheter angiography about 0.5-1 mL/min. CTA is first line in unstable patients. DSA allows superselective microcoil or particle embolisation. Scintigraphy localises poorly.

q: A dreaded complication of bronchial artery embolisation is:
e: Bronchial arteries may share an origin with the anterior spinal artery.
p: Bronchial arteries arise at about T5-T6. Non-bronchial systemic collaterals (intercostal, internal mammary, inferior phrenic) are common. Identify the spinal supply before embolising, use a microcatheter and avoid very small particles.

q: The ideal tip position for a tunnelled central venous catheter is the:
o: Cavoatrial junction or upper right atrium
e: The cavoatrial junction gives good flow with low thrombosis risk.
p: Right IJ is preferred (straight path), with ultrasound guidance. Subclavian access raises pneumothorax and stenosis risk. Avoid the right ventricle (arrhythmia, perforation). Dialysis catheters sit lower in the right atrium.

q: Which is part of the rule of 6s for a mature AV fistula?
e: Diameter 6 mm or more, depth 6 mm or less, flow 600 mL/min or more, within 6 weeks.
p: Stenosis most often occurs at the juxta-anastomotic and outflow segments. Treat with high-pressure balloon angioplasty. Intervene for 50% stenosis with a clinical or haemodynamic abnormality.

q: The most common complication of CT-guided lung biopsy is:
e: Pneumothorax occurs in a substantial minority of biopsies.
p: Risks: emphysema, small deep lesions, long needle paths, crossing fissures, multiple pleural passes. Air embolism is rare but catastrophic (stroke): give 100% oxygen and consider hyperbaric therapy.

q: The heat-sink effect in thermal ablation refers to:
o: Cooling by blood flow in adjacent vessels, causing incomplete ablation
e: Flowing blood carries heat away from tumours near large vessels.
p: Microwave ablation is less affected. Cryoablation shows an ice ball on CT or ultrasound. Aim for a margin of about 5-10 mm around the tumour.

q: The most common type of bladder rupture in trauma, usually with pelvic fracture, is:
e: Extraperitoneal rupture accounts for most cases.
p: CT cystography needs retrograde filling (about 250-350 mL). Intraperitoneal rupture (dome) outlines bowel loops and needs surgery. Extraperitoneal gives flame-shaped extravasation and is usually catheter-managed. Blood at the meatus: urethrogram first.

q: An SMA embolus in acute mesenteric ischaemia typically lodges:
o: 3-10 cm beyond the origin, past the middle colic
e: Emboli lodge distal to the middle colic, sparing proximal jejunal branches; thrombosis occurs at the origin.
p: CTA: filling defect, bowel wall thickening or non-enhancement, pneumatosis, portal venous gas. Treat with revascularisation, laparotomy for dead bowel, or catheter-directed aspiration or thrombolysis.

q: Which finding is part of the CT hypovolaemic shock complex?
e: A collapsed IVC with diffuse bowel enhancement points to hypoperfusion.
p: Also: intensely enhancing small bowel mucosa with fluid-filled loops, collapsed aorta, hyperenhancing adrenals, peripancreatic fluid. A distended IVC suggests right heart failure instead.

q: A Chance fracture results from:
e: Seat-belt flexion-distraction splits the vertebra horizontally.
p: Look for associated bowel and mesenteric injury and the seat-belt sign. Jefferson fracture: axial load, C1 ring (combined lateral mass overhang over 7 mm suggests transverse ligament rupture). Hangman: C2 pars fracture.

q: Which is NOT a typical anterior mediastinal mass?
e: Neurogenic tumours are posterior mediastinal.
p: Anterior: thymoma, teratoma, thyroid, lymphoma. Middle: nodes, bronchogenic cyst. Posterior: schwannoma, neuroblastoma in children. Thymoma associates with myasthenia gravis.

q: Multiple pulmonary arteriovenous malformations strongly suggest:
e: Most pulmonary AVMs occur in HHT.
p: Risk is paradoxical embolism: stroke and brain abscess. Treat feeding arteries of 2-3 mm or more by embolisation (coils or vascular plugs). Screen for brain AVMs. Curacao criteria apply.

q: A typical amoebic liver abscess is:
o: Solitary, right lobe, near the capsule
e: Amoebic abscess is usually solitary, in the right lobe, peripheral and gas-free.
p: Pyogenic abscess: cluster sign, often biliary or portal source. Amoebic: metronidazole; drain only if large, refractory, left lobe or at risk of rupture. Hydatid: daughter cysts, water lily sign.

q: Tumour contact with the SMA exceeding what degree defines locally advanced (unresectable) pancreatic cancer?
e: More than 180 degrees of SMA contact is locally advanced.
p: Borderline resectable: SMA contact 180 degrees or less, or reconstructable venous involvement. Use a pancreatic-protocol CT. Typical lesion is hypoattenuating, with the double duct sign.

q: On rectal MRI, tumour within what distance of the mesorectal fascia means a threatened CRM?
e: 1 mm or less is threatened; 1-2 mm is marginal.
p: Use high-resolution T2 axial images perpendicular to the tumour. T3 is subdivided by extramural depth. Assess EMVI. Nodes are judged by border and signal, not size alone.

q: The commonest bladder cancer histology in developed countries is:
e: Urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma.
p: Squamous histology is linked to schistosomiasis and chronic irritation. Adenocarcinoma: urachal remnant at the dome. CT urography evaluates the upper tract; VI-RADS assesses muscle invasion on MRI.

q: Which adrenal lesion contains macroscopic fat?
e: Myelolipoma contains fat and haematopoietic tissue.
p: Fat is below -20 HU. Lipid-poor adenomas lack macroscopic fat. Adrenocortical carcinoma is large and heterogeneous. Myelolipomas can haemorrhage.

q: Neuropathic (Charcot) arthropathy in diabetes most commonly involves the:
e: The midfoot, especially the Lisfranc joint, is most often affected.
p: Features: disorganisation, debris, dislocation, fragmentation, sclerosis. Osteomyelitis instead arises contiguous to a skin ulcer with confluent low T1 marrow signal. Charcot is periarticular and multifocal.

q: Modic type 2 endplate change shows:
e: Type 2 is fatty marrow replacement.
p: Type 1: oedema, T1 low and T2 high, often enhancing. Type 3: sclerosis, low on both. Discitis shows a T2-bright disc with endplate erosion and enhancement.

q: The most specific radiographic sign of necrotising enterocolitis is:
e: Intramural gas is the most specific sign.
p: Portal venous gas gives branching lucencies to the liver periphery. Pneumoperitoneum (football sign) means perforation. Preterm infants are at risk. Ultrasound shows wall thickening and absent perfusion.

q: A lucent, rim-calcified mass after breast surgery most likely represents:
e: Fat necrosis forms oil cysts with eggshell calcification.
p: Benign, BI-RADS 2 when typical. Fat necrosis can mimic a mass or distortion early and calcify later.

q: Chemical shift artefact of the first kind occurs along the:
e: Fat and water resonate at different frequencies, shifting them along the frequency axis.
p: Fat resonates about 3.5 ppm lower than water; the shift grows with field strength and shrinks with a higher receiver bandwidth. The second kind (India ink) appears at fat-water interfaces on opposed-phase gradient echo.

q: The best-supported prophylaxis against contrast-associated AKI in high-risk patients is:
e: IV isotonic hydration is recommended; N-acetylcysteine adds no proven benefit.
p: Prophylaxis is advised for eGFR under 30 or AKI, and is not required for eGFR 45 or above. Use the lowest necessary contrast volume.

q: The lambda (twin peak) sign indicates:
e: Chorionic tissue extends into the base of the intertwin membrane.
p: The T sign indicates monochorionic twins. Determine chorionicity in the first trimester. Monochorionic twins risk TTTS; monoamniotic twins risk cord entanglement.

q: In pc-ASPECTS (posterior circulation), which regions carry 2 points each?
e: Midbrain and pons score 2 each; thalami, cerebellar hemispheres and PCA territories score 1 each (total 10).
p: Basilar occlusion thrombectomy was shown beneficial within 12 h in ATTENTION and BAOCHE (2022), after earlier negative trials (BEST, BASICS). Lower pc-ASPECTS predicts poor outcome.

q: Modified Fisher grade 3 SAH is:
e: Grade 3 is thick cisternal blood without IVH; grade 4 is thick SAH with IVH.
p: Grades 1-2 are thin SAH (without or with IVH). Higher grade predicts delayed cerebral ischaemia, peaking days 4-14. Nimodipine is standard. Thick is blood of about 1 mm or more filling a cistern or fissure.

q: ISAT compared with clipping, endovascular coiling of ruptured aneurysms showed:
o: Lower death or dependency at 1 year, with higher late rebleeding
Higher death or dependency at 1 year
e: Coiling gave better 1-year functional outcome but more late rebleeds and retreatment.
p: ISAT enrolled aneurysms suitable for either treatment, mostly small anterior circulation. Flow diverters suit wide-neck or fusiform aneurysms; WEB devices suit wide-neck bifurcation aneurysms.

q: Bilateral paramedian thalamic infarcts with midbrain involvement (V sign) suggest occlusion of the:
e: A single P1 branch supplies both paramedian thalami.
p: Presents with vertical gaze palsy, hypersomnolence, amnesia. Deep venous thrombosis is a mimic. Heubner supplies the caudate head and anterior internal capsule; anterior choroidal supplies the posterior limb of the internal capsule.

q: The hockey-stick sign (pulvinar plus dorsomedial thalamus on DWI/T2) is associated with:
e: The pulvinar and hockey-stick signs are characteristic of variant CJD.
p: Sporadic CJD: cortical ribboning and striatal restricted diffusion on DWI, with periodic sharp waves on EEG. RT-QuIC on CSF supports diagnosis.

q: The most common spinal vascular malformation is:
e: Type I dural AV fistula, typically in older men at the thoracolumbar level.
p: Venous hypertension gives central cord T2 hyperintensity with dorsal flow voids. The fistula sits at the nerve root sleeve and is found on spinal angiography; treat by embolisation or surgery. The syndrome is Foix-Alajouanine.

q: In an immunocompetent adult, primary CNS lymphoma typically shows:
e: Hypercellular lymphoma enhances homogeneously and restricts diffusion, often periventricular and hyperdense on CT.
p: In AIDS it may ring-enhance and mimic toxoplasmosis (eccentric target sign; thallium or PET negative). Steroids can cause regression, so avoid before biopsy.

q: In idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus, the callosal angle is typically:
e: A callosal angle under 90 degrees supports iNPH.
p: Also Evans index above 0.3 and the DESH pattern: enlarged sylvian fissures with tight high-convexity sulci. Hakim triad: gait disturbance, dementia, incontinence. CSF tap test predicts shunt response.

q: The most common endoleak after EVAR is:
e: Type II is retrograde flow from branches such as lumbar arteries or the IMA.
p: Type I (attachment site) and III (graft junction or fabric tear) need urgent treatment. IV: graft porosity. V: endotension. Intervene on type II if the sac grows by 5 mm or more; embolise via transarterial or translumbar routes.

q: Rutherford IIb acute limb ischaemia is characterised by:
o: Sensory loss beyond the toes, mild-moderate weakness, inaudible arterial Doppler
No sensory loss, audible arterial signal
Profound paralysis with no arterial or venous Doppler signals
Minimal toe sensory loss, no weakness
e: IIb is immediately threatened and needs urgent revascularisation.
p: I viable; IIa marginally threatened (minimal toe sensory loss, no weakness); III irreversible (paralysis, no venous signal), which means amputation. Catheter-directed thrombolysis is contraindicated with active bleeding or recent intracranial haemorrhage or stroke.

q: In May-Thurner syndrome the left common iliac vein is compressed by the:
e: The right common iliac artery compresses it against the lumbosacral spine.
p: Typical patient: young woman with left leg DVT. IVUS beats venography for diagnosis. After clearing thrombus, treat with a self-expanding venous stent.

q: In median arcuate ligament syndrome, coeliac artery narrowing on lateral aortography typically:
e: Expiration moves the ligament caudally and increases the hooked compression.
p: Look for the hooked appearance on lateral view. Stenting alone is generally avoided, since the artery is recompressed; treatment is surgical release. Also called Dunbar syndrome.

q: Y-90 radioembolisation is generally contraindicated when the lung shunt fraction exceeds about:
e: Above about 20% (or a lung dose over 30 Gy per session).
p: Shunt is assessed with Tc-99m MAA. Prophylactic embolisation of the gastroduodenal and right gastric arteries prevents GI deposition. Y-90 is a pure beta emitter with a half-life of 64 hours.

q: Bismuth-Corlette type II hilar cholangiocarcinoma involves:
o: Common hepatic duct below the confluence
The confluence plus the right hepatic duct
e: Type II reaches the confluence without extending into the secondary ducts.
p: I: below the confluence. IIIa: right duct. IIIb: left duct. IV: both, or multifocal. In biliary drainage, drain the future liver remnant and avoid contrast in undrained segments.

q: Effort thrombosis (Paget-Schroetter) is typically treated with:
o: Catheter-directed thrombolysis then first rib decompression
Primary stenting of the subclavian vein
e: Lysis restores flow, then decompression removes the compression.
p: Typical patients are young, active arm users. Stents placed in an extrinsically compressed vein fail, so decompress first. Venography with arm abduction shows the compression.

q: Minimally invasive adenocarcinoma is defined as lepidic predominant, 3 cm or less, with an invasive focus of:
e: Invasion must be 5 mm or less.
p: Adenocarcinoma in situ is pure lepidic, 3 cm or less. A persistent part-solid nodule of 6 mm or more needs CT at 3-6 months, then annual follow-up for up to 5 years. A solid component over 6 mm is highly suspicious.

q: The headcheese (three-density) sign is classically seen in:
e: Normal, ground-glass and air-trapped lobules in one lung give a three-density pattern.
p: Fibrotic HP: centrilobular nodules, mosaic attenuation with air-trapping, mid to upper zone or peribronchovascular fibrosis. Sarcoid and small airways disease can also produce it. UIP is basal and subpleural.

q: On gadoxetate hepatobiliary phase, FNH typically appears:
e: FNH contains functioning hepatocytes and biliary elements.
p: HCC, adenoma and metastases are usually hypointense. Exceptions: some well-differentiated HCCs and beta-catenin-activated adenomas can be iso- or hyperintense. A scar may be hypointense.

q: Which feature favours mucinous cystic neoplasm over IPMN?
o: Middle-aged woman, body or tail, no ductal communication
e: MCN has ovarian-type stroma and does not communicate with the duct.
p: IPMN communicates with the main duct or branches. Serous cystadenoma: microcystic honeycomb with a central scar. MCN usually shows a peripheral eggshell calcification and thick-walled macrocysts.

q: Groove pancreatitis typically shows:
o: Soft tissue in the pancreaticoduodenal groove with duodenal wall cysts
e: Sheet-like tissue in the groove with cystic change in the duodenal wall.
p: Associated with alcohol use. Can mimic head carcinoma; the groove tissue is delayed-enhancing and the common bile duct may taper smoothly. Duodenal stenosis is possible.

q: On MRI, a junctional zone thickness suggesting adenomyosis is about:
e: 12 mm or more is diagnostic; 8-12 mm is indeterminate.
p: Look for T2-dark myometrial thickening with small bright cystic foci. A focal adenomyoma lacks a capsule and is ill-defined, unlike a fibroid.

q: Which feature favours low-grade chondrosarcoma over enchondroma?
o: Endosteal scalloping over two-thirds of cortical thickness
e: Deep endosteal scalloping suggests chondrosarcoma.
p: Other pointers: pain without a fracture, size over 5-6 cm, soft-tissue mass, cortical destruction, active uptake. Enchondromas are usually asymptomatic.

q: Chiari I malformation is defined by tonsillar descent of at least:
e: Tonsils 5 mm or more below the foramen magnum.
p: Associated with syrinx and basilar invagination. Chiari II: myelomeningocele, beaked tectum, lacunar skull.

q: A hyperdense midline lesion at the foramen of Monro with hydrocephalus is most likely a:
e: Colloid cysts sit in the anterosuperior third ventricle and obstruct both foramina.
p: Hyperdense on CT in most; T2 signal is variable. Risk of acute hydrocephalus and sudden death. Central neurocytoma attaches to the septum with a bubbly look.

q: Oligodendroglioma (WHO 2021) is defined by:
o: IDH wildtype with TERT promoter mutation
e: IDH-mutant with 1p/19q codeletion.
p: Typically frontal, cortical-subcortical, calcified. IDH-wildtype with TERT mutation is glioblastoma. H3 K27M defines diffuse midline glioma.

q: T2 hyperintensities in the anterior temporal poles and external capsules suggest:
e: The anterior temporal pole and external capsule pattern is classic for CADASIL.
p: NOTCH3 mutation. Also lacunes, microbleeds, migraine with aura and early strokes.

q: A tigroid (striated) cerebellar hemisphere mass is typical of Lhermitte-Duclos disease, which is associated with:
e: Dysplastic cerebellar gangliocytoma goes with PTEN hamartoma (Cowden) syndrome.
p: Look for breast and thyroid disease in the patient. The lesion is non-enhancing with a striated pattern.

q: Profound acute hypoxic-ischaemic injury in a term neonate characteristically affects:
o: Basal ganglia, thalami and perirolandic cortex
e: Profound acute injury hits metabolically active deep grey matter.
p: Prolonged partial hypoxia causes parasagittal watershed injury. Preterm injury is periventricular leukomalacia. DWI is most useful in the first days.

q: The most important measure to reduce radial artery occlusion after radial access is:
o: Adequate intra-procedural heparin and patent haemostasis
e: Heparin and compression that preserves radial flow lower occlusion.
p: Use the smallest sheath, hydrophilic sheath and vasodilator cocktail. Check ulnar flow beforehand.

q: COMPASS compared first-line direct aspiration with stent retrievers for LVO and found:
e: Aspiration first was non-inferior on mRS 0-2 at 90 days.
p: ASTER found no difference in reperfusion. Combined techniques and balloon guide catheters are common. Choice depends on clot and anatomy.

q: CREST comparing carotid stenting with endarterectomy showed:
o: Higher periprocedural stroke with stenting, higher MI with endarterectomy
Higher stroke and MI with endarterectomy
e: The primary composite endpoint was equivalent, with different periprocedural risk profiles.
p: Older patients (about 70 or more) did better with endarterectomy; younger patients did slightly better with stenting.

q: PEITHO (tenecteplase in intermediate-risk PE) showed:
o: Less haemodynamic decompensation but more major bleeding
e: Systemic lysis reduced decompensation but raised major extracranial bleeding and haemorrhagic stroke.
p: Catheter-directed therapies aim to cut lytic dose. High-risk (massive) PE with shock is the clear indication for lysis.

q: The right gonadal vein drains into the:
e: The right drains into the IVC, the left into the left renal vein.
p: This explains left-sided predominance of varicoceles and gonadal vein embolisation approach via the femoral or jugular vein.

q: Splenic artery aneurysm treatment is indicated for size over:
o: 2 cm, or in pregnancy or women of childbearing age
e: Treat if over 2 cm, symptomatic, pseudoaneurysm, or in pregnancy or childbearing-age women.
p: It is the most common visceral artery aneurysm. Rupture in pregnancy is catastrophic. Treat with coil embolisation or stent graft.

q: CO2 angiography is generally avoided in:
e: Risk of neurotoxicity and air-lock above the diaphragm.
p: CO2 suits renal-impaired patients and iodine allergy below the diaphragm. Avoid in patients with a right-to-left shunt for cerebral risk.

q: The HVPG threshold for clinically significant portal hypertension is:
e: 10 mmHg or more is clinically significant; 12 mmHg or more carries risk of variceal bleeding.
p: Normal is 1-5 mmHg. Measure with a balloon catheter in the wedged hepatic vein. A fall of 20% or to under 12 mmHg is protective.

q: Thin-walled uniform cysts in a young woman with chylous pleural effusion suggest:
e: LAM gives diffuse thin-walled cysts in reproductive-age women.
p: Associated with tuberous sclerosis (angiomyolipomas). Treated with sirolimus. LCH: smokers, upper-zone, bizarre cysts.

q: Upper zone nodules that cavitate and become bizarre cysts, sparing the costophrenic angles, in a smoker suggest:
e: PLCH is the classic smoking-related cystic disease.
p: Evolution: nodules, cavitating nodules, then thick-walled and bizarre cysts. Stopping smoking can lead to regression.

q: Swyer-James (Macleod) syndrome shows:
o: A small hyperlucent lung with air trapping
A large hyperlucent lung with mediastinal shift
e: Unilateral hyperlucency with a small hilum and expiratory air trapping.
p: Post-infectious obliterative bronchiolitis in childhood. Distinguish from pulmonary artery agenesis or a proximal obstructing lesion.

q: Delayed enhancement with capsular retraction in a liver mass suggests:
e: Fibrous stroma gives persistent delayed enhancement.
p: Peripheral enhancement with progressive fill-in. Look for dilated peripheral ducts and satellite nodules. Normal AFP.

q: On small bowel imaging, jejunisation of the ileum with reversed fold pattern suggests:
e: Loss of jejunal folds and prominent ileal folds.
p: Also transient intussusception, hyposplenism, and lymph nodes with fat-fluid levels (cavitating mesenteric lymph node syndrome).

q: Which feature suggests pseudoachalasia from malignancy?
o: Short history and eccentric irregular GOJ narrowing in an older patient
e: A tumour at the gastro-oesophageal junction can mimic achalasia.
p: Primary achalasia: smooth bird-beak, dilated aperistaltic oesophagus. Always correlate with endoscopy and CT when atypical.

q: In pancreas divisum, the dorsal duct drains through the:
e: The duct of Santorini drains via the minor papilla; the ventral duct is small.
p: Most common congenital pancreatic anomaly. Secretin-enhanced MRCP helps. Link to recurrent pancreatitis is debated.

q: The bear paw sign with a staghorn calculus suggests:
e: A non-functioning kidney with hydronephrotic calyces and a staghorn stone.
p: Often Proteus infection. Foamy lipid-laden macrophages. Treated with nephrectomy.

q: International grade II vesicoureteral reflux shows contrast reaching the:
o: Ureter, pelvis and calyces without dilatation
e: Grade II fills the whole collecting system without dilatation.
p: I: ureter only. III: mild dilatation. IV: moderate dilatation with blunting of fornices. V: gross dilatation and tortuosity.

q: The O-RADS US risk of malignancy for category 4 is:
e: Category 4 is intermediate risk.
p: 2: almost certainly benign (under 1%). 3: low (1 to under 10%). 5: high (50% or more).

q: Cervical cancer invading the parametrium but not the pelvic sidewall is FIGO 2018 stage:
e: Parametrial invasion short of the sidewall is IIB.
p: IB1 under 2 cm, IB2 2-under 4 cm, IB3 4 cm or more. IIA: upper two-thirds of vagina. IIIB: sidewall extension or hydronephrosis.

q: A Hill-Sachs lesion is located at the:
e: Impaction against the anterior glenoid during anterior dislocation.
p: Bankart lesion: anteroinferior labrum. Reverse Hill-Sachs follows posterior dislocation (anteromedial). HAGL: humeral avulsion of the inferior glenohumeral ligament.

q: Osteochondritis dissecans of the knee classically involves the:
o: Lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle
Medial aspect of the lateral femoral condyle
e: Classic site is the lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle.
p: Instability signs on MRI: fluid-signal line beneath the fragment, cysts over 5 mm, breached cartilage.

q: The blade of grass (flame) sign in a long bone indicates:
e: Advancing lytic front in a long bone in Paget disease.
p: Phases: lytic, mixed, sclerotic. Look for cotton wool skull, picture-frame vertebra, and sarcomatous change in about 1%.

q: A rectosigmoid index below 1 on barium enema suggests:
e: The aganglionic rectum is narrower than the dilated sigmoid.
p: Look for transition zone and delayed evacuation at 24 hours. Short-segment is commonest; total colonic disease may mimic microcolon.

q: Which sonographic finding supports biliary atresia?
e: Periportal fibrous tissue gives the triangular cord sign.
p: Also a small or absent gallbladder and no excretion on HIDA after phenobarbital. Early Kasai surgery improves outcomes.

q: Papile grade II intraventricular haemorrhage is:
e: Blood fills the ventricle without dilating it.
p: I: subependymal (germinal matrix). III: IVH with dilatation. IV: parenchymal venous infarction.

q: Compared with ductal carcinoma, invasive lobular carcinoma is more likely to be:
e: Single-file growth causes subtle findings.
p: MRI finds more disease. Architectural distortion or asymmetry on mammography; irregular hypoechoic mass with shadowing on US.

q: A rapidly growing large, lobulated breast mass with leaf-like clefts suggests:
e: Phyllodes tumours have a leaf-like architecture and grow fast.
p: Imaging cannot reliably separate benign from malignant phyllodes. Excise with wide margins.

q: DLP in CT equals CTDIvol multiplied by:
e: DLP = CTDIvol x scan length.
p: Effective dose is estimated as DLP times a body-region conversion factor k. CTDIvol is not patient dose.

q: ACR Group II gadolinium agents have:
e: Group II agents (for example gadobutrol, gadoterate) carry an extremely low NSF risk.
p: Group I (gadodiamide and similar) carries the highest NSF risk. Macrocyclic agents are more stable.

q: Which tumour commonly gives false-negative FDG-PET?
e: Low cellularity and mucin reduce FDG uptake.
p: Other false negatives: lepidic adenocarcinoma, carcinoid, well-differentiated HCC, and lesions under about 8 mm.

q: A cervical length under what value before 24 weeks raises preterm birth risk?
e: Under 25 mm is considered short.
p: Measure transvaginally. Management includes vaginal progesterone and cerclage in selected cases.

q: How many parameters make up the biophysical profile?
e: NST, breathing, movement, tone and amniotic fluid (2 points each, maximum 10).
p: A score of 8-10 is reassuring, 6 is equivocal and 4 or less is concerning. Fluid is the chronic marker.

q: Epiploic appendagitis typically shows:
o: Oval fat-attenuation lesion with a hyperattenuating ring and central dot
e: Inflamed fat with a thin ring and central thrombosed vessel.
p: Self-limited and treated conservatively. Mimics diverticulitis or appendicitis clinically.

q: In ovarian torsion, Doppler flow:
o: May be normal because of dual blood supply
e: Normal Doppler does not exclude torsion.
p: Look for an enlarged oedematous ovary with peripheral follicles, whirlpool sign of the pedicle and deviated uterus. Surgical detorsion is urgent.

q: A lesion is bright on DWI. Which finding best identifies T2 shine-through rather than true restricted diffusion?
e: T2 shine-through is bright on DWI because of high T2, but ADC is not low.
p: Always read DWI with the ADC map. Chronic infarcts and vasogenic oedema are DWI-bright through T2 effect. True restriction: acute infarct, abscess, epidermoid, lymphoma, CJD.

q: On SWI phase images, calcification is distinguished from haemorrhage because calcium is:
o: Diamagnetic, giving opposite phase to blood products
e: Blood products are paramagnetic and calcium is diamagnetic, so their phase signs are opposite.
p: Both bloom on magnitude images. Use phase images or CT to separate them. This helps in cavernoma versus calcified lesions.

q: A longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis with an area postrema lesion most suggests:
e: NMOSD classically gives cord lesions of 3 or more vertebral segments, optic neuritis and area postrema syndrome.
p: MS lesions are short, peripheral and dorsolateral. MOGAD can resemble NMOSD with conus involvement. Spinal dural AVF mimics LETM but shows dorsal flow voids.

q: A Zabramski type IV cavernous malformation is characterised by:
o: Punctate lesions visible only on GRE or SWI
A popcorn lesion with mixed signal and a haemosiderin rim
A subacute haemorrhage with T1 hyperintense core
A chronic haemorrhage with a haemosiderin-stained cavity
e: Type IV lesions are tiny punctate foci seen only on blood-sensitive sequences.
p: Type I: subacute haemorrhage. II: classic popcorn. III: chronic haemosiderin, low on T2 and GRE. Multiple lesions suggest a familial form (CCM1-3).

q: Why should a developmental venous anomaly not be embolised or resected?
o: It drains normal brain and removal risks venous infarction
e: A DVA is normal venous drainage in an anatomical variant.
p: Caput medusae with a large draining vein. Coexisting cavernoma is the lesion that bleeds. Venous infarction can follow DVA thrombosis.

q: Thunderclap headache with a normal initial CT and multifocal segmental vasoconstriction that resolves in weeks suggests:
e: Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome resolves over 1-3 months.
p: Triggers: vasoactive drugs, postpartum state. Complications: convexity SAH, ICH, PRES, infarction. Steroids can worsen it. Vasculitis shows persistent stenoses and wall enhancement.

q: In suspected heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, the correct first step is to:
o: Stop all heparin, including flushes and coated catheters, and start a non-heparin anticoagulant
e: All heparin exposure must stop; use argatroban or bivalirudin.
p: Typical onset 5-10 days, platelet fall over 50%, with thrombosis risk. LMWH cross-reacts. Use the 4Ts score to judge probability. Relevant for IR flush solutions and heparin-coated catheters.

q: Thrombin injection of a femoral pseudoaneurysm is most likely to fail or cause distal embolisation when the:
e: A short wide neck allows thrombin to escape into the parent artery.
p: Technique: ultrasound-guided, needle tip in the sac away from the neck, small doses (about 0.5-1 mL of 1000 U/mL). Monitor distal pulses. Treat with compression or surgery if unsuitable.

q: On inferior petrosal sinus sampling for Cushing disease, a pituitary source is indicated by an IPS:peripheral ACTH ratio of at least:
e: A gradient of 2 or more at baseline, or 3 or more after CRH, localises to the pituitary.
p: Compare left and right sides for lateralisation, though accuracy is limited. Venous anatomy variants and technical failure give false results. Prolactin normalisation checks catheter position.

q: A MELD score above about what predicts high early mortality after elective TIPS?
e: MELD above about 18 predicts poor outcome.
p: Other poor prognostic features: bilirubin above 3-5 mg/dL, severe encephalopathy, heart failure. Covered stents reduce dysfunction. Rescue TIPS for bleeding is a different context.

q: An ankle-brachial index above 1.3 suggests:
e: Calcified vessels cannot be compressed, falsely raising the index.
p: Measure toe-brachial index or use waveform analysis in diabetics and renal patients. Normal ABI is 1.0-1.3.

q: Symptomatic chronic mesenteric ischaemia usually requires significant disease in:
o: At least two of the three mesenteric vessels
e: Rich collaterals mean single-vessel disease is rarely symptomatic.
p: Typical story: postprandial pain, food fear, weight loss. CTA shows the stenoses and collaterals (arc of Riolan, marginal artery). Treat by angioplasty and stenting or bypass.

q: CORAL compared renal artery stenting plus medical therapy with medical therapy alone and showed:
o: No added benefit of stenting for cardiovascular or renal events
e: Stenting added no benefit in atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis.
p: Selected situations (flash pulmonary oedema, rapidly declining function) were not well studied. FMD is treated differently, with angioplasty.

q: Chemical shift MRI helps differentiate thymic hyperplasia from thymoma because hyperplasia shows:
e: Microscopic fat in hyperplasia gives signal loss on opposed-phase imaging.
p: Thymic rebound follows chemotherapy or steroid withdrawal. Thymoma does not drop signal. The gland keeps its normal shape in hyperplasia.

q: Lung-RADS v2022 category 4A for a new solid nodule is:
e: 4A is a baseline solid nodule of 8 to under 15 mm.
p: 3: 6 to under 8 mm. 4B: 15 mm or more. NLST showed 20% lung cancer mortality reduction with LDCT. New nodules have different size thresholds.

q: High-attenuation mucus within central bronchiectasis in an asthmatic suggests:
e: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis gives central upper lobe bronchiectasis with high-attenuation mucus.
p: Finger-in-glove opacities are mucoid impaction. Cystic fibrosis shows upper lobe predominance with peripheral disease. Kartagener syndrome has situs inversus.

q: A sausage-shaped diffusely enlarged pancreas with a capsule-like rim suggests:
e: Type 1 AIP (IgG4) gives diffuse enlargement with a delayed-enhancing rim.
p: Responds to steroids. May involve the bile duct (long stricture), kidneys, retroperitoneum. Focal AIP can mimic cancer.

q: Ischaemic colitis most often affects which watershed zones?
e: Griffiths point (splenic flexure) and Sudeck point (rectosigmoid) are watershed regions.
p: Rectal sparing suggests ischaemia over inflammatory bowel disease. Thumbprinting with segmental wall thickening is typical.

q: The water lily sign in hydatid disease reflects:
e: The detached membrane floats within the fluid, indicating a degenerating cyst.
p: WHO stages: CE1-CE2 active, CE3 transitional (CE3a detached membrane, CE3b daughter cysts in solid matrix), CE4-CE5 inactive. Percutaneous PAIR needs an active stage and avoids communicating biliary cysts.

q: The goblet sign in the ureter indicates:
o: A urothelial tumour with a dilated ureter below it
e: Contrast outlines the tumour cap, like a goblet.
p: The filling defect is intraluminal and expands the ureter. Compare with stone (rim sign) and pyeloureteritis cystica (multiple small filling defects).

q: A testicular epidermoid cyst typically shows:
o: An onion-ring pattern and no vascularity
e: Concentric keratin layers give an onion-ring appearance, avascular on Doppler.
p: Benign. Testis-sparing surgery is possible. Elastography shows a hard lesion despite benign nature.

q: The anteater sign on a lateral foot radiograph indicates:
e: An elongated anterior process of the calcaneus resembles an anteater nose.
p: Talocalcaneal coalition: C sign, talar beak, and dysmorphic sustentaculum. CT or MRI defines the type of coalition.

q: Which is a Kocher criterion for septic arthritis of the hip in a child?
e: The four are non-weight-bearing, fever over 38.5, ESR over 40 and WBC over 12,000.
p: More criteria means higher probability. Ultrasound shows effusion but cannot tell septic from transient synovitis. Aspiration is definitive.

q: On an upper GI study, the duodenojejunal flexure in a normal infant lies:
o: To the left of the left pedicle at the level of the duodenal bulb
To the right of the spine
Below the pylorus on the right
e: It should lie left of the left vertebral pedicle and at the duodenal bulb level.
p: Malrotation: abnormal position, corkscrew duodenum with volvulus. Treatment is the Ladd procedure. Feeding intolerance with bilious vomiting is a surgical emergency.

q: On Graf hip ultrasound, a normal mature hip has an alpha angle of at least:
e: Type I hips have alpha 60 degrees or more.
p: IIa: 50-59 degrees in an infant under 3 months (physiological immaturity). Beta angle is also assessed. Standard views require a correct coronal plane at the mid-acetabulum.

q: The Nyquist limit in Doppler ultrasound equals:
e: Aliasing occurs when the Doppler shift exceeds half the pulse repetition frequency.
p: Reduce aliasing by raising PRF (scale), lowering baseline shift, lowering transducer frequency, or using continuous wave. Lower frequency decreases the Doppler shift.

q: The best radiopharmaceutical for demonstrating renal cortical scarring is:
e: DMSA binds proximal tubular cells and shows cortical defects.
p: MAG3: tubular secretion, drainage and differential function. DTPA: glomerular filtration. Scarring scans are best 4-6 months after infection.

q: The snowstorm sign on ultrasound indicates:
e: Free silicone gives echogenic noise with posterior shadowing.
p: Intracapsular rupture: stepladder sign on US, linguine sign on MRI. Contrast is not required for MRI implant assessment.

q: In stroke of unknown onset, a DWI-positive, FLAIR-negative mismatch suggests the infarct is likely within about:
e: FLAIR changes lag behind DWI, so a mismatch suggests onset within about 4.5 hours.
p: WAKE-UP showed benefit of thrombolysis guided by DWI-FLAIR mismatch. Wake-up and unwitnessed strokes can be selected this way. Perfusion imaging extends EVT selection to 24 hours.

q: RAPID CT perfusion defines ischaemic core as rCBF below:
e: Core is rCBF under 30%; hypoperfusion is Tmax over 6 seconds.
p: DEFUSE-3 mismatch: core under 70 mL, ratio 1.8 or more, mismatch volume 15 mL or more. Penumbra equals hypoperfusion minus core. Motion and arch occlusions cause pitfalls.

q: Mesial temporal sclerosis typically shows:
o: Small hippocampus with T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and lost internal architecture
e: Atrophy plus T2/FLAIR bright signal and loss of digitations.
