p: Use thin coronal T2 and FLAIR perpendicular to the hippocampus. Ipsilateral fornix and mammillary body atrophy support it. Dual pathology can coexist.

q: Basal meningeal enhancement with hydrocephalus and basal ganglia infarcts suggests:
e: The triad is basal enhancement, hydrocephalus and infarcts.
p: Infarcts involve the TB zone (medial striate and thalamoperforating arteries). Tuberculomas appear as ring or solid enhancing nodules. Sarcoid and fungal disease also cause basal enhancement.

q: A cyst with an eccentric scolex (dot-in-a-hole), no enhancement and no oedema is which stage of neurocysticercosis?
e: The living larva evokes little reaction in the vesicular stage.
p: Colloidal: ring enhancement with oedema as the larva dies. Granular nodular: shrinking enhancing nodule. Calcified: residual calcification, seizure focus. Treat with albendazole plus steroids in selected stages.

q: A non-enhancing isointense lesion at the tuber cinereum with gelastic seizures is a:
e: Hypothalamic hamartoma classically causes gelastic seizures and precocious puberty.
p: Isointense on T1, iso to hyperintense on T2, non-enhancing, stable over time. Treated with ablation or disconnection.

q: Papillary craniopharyngioma is characterised by:
o: Adult patients, mainly solid, BRAF V600E mutation
Children, calcified and cystic, CTNNB1 mutation
e: Papillary type is a solid adult tumour with BRAF V600E.
p: Adamantinomatous type: children, cystic with calcification, machinery-oil fluid, CTNNB1 mutation. Both sit in the suprasellar region.

q: Which feature separates a cerebellopontine angle epidermoid from an arachnoid cyst?
o: Restricted diffusion and incomplete FLAIR suppression
e: Epidermoids restrict diffusion and do not suppress fully on FLAIR; arachnoid cysts follow CSF.
p: Epidermoids insinuate around vessels and nerves. Arachnoid cysts displace structures. CISS or FIESTA shows an epidermoid as slightly different from CSF.

q: SAMMPRIS compared stenting plus aggressive medical therapy with aggressive medical therapy alone in symptomatic 70-99% intracranial stenosis and found:
o: Higher 30-day stroke or death with stenting
e: Early periprocedural events were higher with stenting.
p: The trial was stopped early. Aggressive medical therapy (dual antiplatelet therapy for 90 days, risk control) did better than expected. Later data (WEAVE) address selected cases.

q: Dual antiplatelet therapy is required after flow-diverter placement mainly to prevent:
o: Thrombosis of the device or parent artery
e: The metal surface is thrombogenic until endothelialised.
p: Flow diverters suit wide-neck, large or giant, fusiform or sidewall aneurysms. Risks: ischaemic stroke, delayed aneurysm rupture, perforator occlusion. Response to clopidogrel is sometimes tested.

q: Venous sinus stenting for idiopathic intracranial hypertension is considered when a transverse sinus stenosis has a pressure gradient of about:
e: A gradient across the stenosis of about 8 mmHg or more.
p: Reserved for medically refractory IIH with vision at risk. Venography with manometry confirms the gradient. Complications: stent thrombosis, adjacent stenosis.

q: The main embolisation target in refractory posterior epistaxis is the:
e: The sphenopalatine artery supplies the posterior nasal cavity.
p: Anterior ethmoidal branches come from the ophthalmic artery and are not embolised. Look for dangerous ECA-ICA anastomoses before embolisation. Use particles or coils, avoiding very small embolic particles.

q: EVAR-1 comparing EVAR with open aneurysm repair showed:
o: Lower early mortality with EVAR but no long-term all-cause survival benefit
e: EVAR reduced 30-day operative mortality but not long-term overall survival.
p: EVAR has more reinterventions (endoleak, graft complications) and needs surveillance. Aneurysm-related mortality benefit was early.

q: In cryoablation, the edge of the visible ice ball corresponds to about:
o: 0 C, with the lethal zone inside it
e: The ice ball margin is at 0 C; lethal temperatures lie several millimetres within.
p: Lethal temperatures are about -20 to -40 C. Use two freeze-thaw cycles and extend the ice ball beyond the tumour margin. The ice ball is seen clearly on CT, MRI and ultrasound (acoustic shadow).

q: Subclavian steal syndrome involves:
o: Reversed flow in the ipsilateral vertebral artery
Reversed flow in the carotid artery
Venous reflux in the jugular vein
Reversed flow in the internal mammary artery only
e: A proximal subclavian stenosis draws blood retrograde through the vertebral artery.
p: More common on the left. Blood pressure differs between arms. Treated with angioplasty and stenting or bypass.

q: The split pleura sign on contrast CT indicates:
e: Enhancing thickened visceral and parietal pleura separated by fluid.
p: Empyema features: lenticular loculation, compressed lung, extrapleural fat thickening. Pleural infection may need drainage, fibrinolytics or surgery.

q: Which CT finding favours chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension?
o: Mosaic perfusion with eccentric webs or bands
e: Mosaic attenuation, eccentric thrombus, webs and bronchial artery hypertrophy.
p: Also enlarged main pulmonary artery. V/Q scan is the screening test of choice. Treatment: pulmonary endarterectomy, balloon pulmonary angioplasty (IR), riociguat.

q: In primary haemochromatosis, MRI typically shows low signal in the liver and:
e: Parenchymal iron overload spares the reticuloendothelial system.
p: Transfusional iron overload affects the liver, spleen and marrow. Risk of HCC. Use T2* and in-phase versus opposed-phase signal loss for quantification.

q: The aortomesenteric angle in superior mesenteric artery syndrome is typically under about:
e: Normal is about 25-60 degrees; under about 22 degrees narrows the third part of the duodenum.
p: Aortomesenteric distance is also reduced (under about 8 mm). Associated with weight loss and scoliosis surgery. CT or barium shows abrupt duodenal cut-off.

q: The keyhole sign on ultrasound or VCUG indicates:
e: A dilated posterior urethra with a thick-walled bladder.
p: Look for bilateral hydronephrosis, bladder wall thickening and vesicoureteral reflux in a male infant. Diagnosis is confirmed on VCUG.

q: A T2-dark ovarian mass with ascites and a right pleural effusion suggests:
e: Meigs syndrome is a benign ovarian fibroma with ascites and pleural effusion.
p: Resolves after resection. Fibromas are T2-dark with weak enhancement. Pseudo-Meigs describes other tumours.

q: A lytic epiphyseal lesion with surrounding marrow oedema in a skeletally immature patient suggests:
e: Chondroblastoma arises in the epiphysis before physeal closure.
p: Giant cell tumour occurs after physeal closure. Chondroblastoma has intense surrounding oedema and a thin sclerotic rim. Common at the proximal humerus and femur.

q: Scheuermann disease is defined by wedging of at least:
e: Wedging of 5 degrees or more in at least 3 adjacent vertebrae.
p: Thoracic kyphosis, endplate irregularity and Schmorl nodes. Occurs in adolescents.

q: The most common oesophageal atresia variant is:
o: Proximal blind pouch with distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula
e: Gross type C accounts for most cases.
p: Gas in the stomach indicates a distal fistula. VACTERL association. H-type presents later with recurrent aspiration.

q: SAR in MRI scales with the:
o: Square of the static magnetic field strength
e: SAR rises with the square of B0 and of the flip angle.
p: This is why 3 T scanners limit sequence choice. Reduce SAR with lower flip angles, longer TR, parallel imaging.

q: A central intraductal papilloma most commonly presents with:
e: Solitary central papillomas present with bloody nipple discharge.
p: US shows a mass within a dilated duct. Peripheral multiple papillomas carry higher risk. Papilloma with atypia needs excision.

q: Symmetric FDG uptake in the supraclavicular and paravertebral regions suggests:
e: Brown fat activated by cold gives a symmetric pattern.
p: Reduce by warming the patient before the scan. Beta-blockers may reduce uptake. CT shows fat attenuation at the site.

q: Vasa previa is defined by:
o: Unprotected fetal vessels crossing the internal os
e: Fetal vessels run through membranes over the internal os.
p: Associated with velamentous cord insertion and low-lying placenta. Colour Doppler diagnoses. Planned caesarean at 34 to 37 weeks avoids fetal exsanguination.

q: Mid-wall late gadolinium enhancement in the septum most suggests:
e: Mid-wall septal LGE is typical of dilated cardiomyopathy.
p: Ischaemic: subendocardial to transmural. Myocarditis: subepicardial. Amyloid: diffuse subendocardial with abnormal nulling.

q: Dandy-Walker malformation is characterised by:
o: Vermian hypoplasia with upward rotation, cystic fourth ventricle and high torcula
Complete vermian agenesis with molar tooth sign
Enlarged vermis with small fourth ventricle
e: Vermian hypoplasia and rotation with a cystic fourth ventricle in an enlarged posterior fossa.
p: The torcula-lambdoid inversion (high torcula) separates it from mega cisterna magna. Molar tooth sign: Joubert syndrome. Hydrocephalus is common.

q: Which finding is part of the SEEPS mnemonic of intracranial hypotension?
e: SEEPS: Subdural collections, Enhancement of pachymeninges, Engorged venous structures, Pituitary hyperaemia, Sagging brain.
p: The enhancement is diffuse, smooth and pachymeningeal. Look for a CSF leak (spine MRI, CT myelography). Chiari-like sagging is a mimic of Chiari I.

q: A salt-and-pepper appearance on MRI in a jugular foramen mass suggests:
e: Flow voids give the pepper and haemorrhage or avid enhancement the salt.
p: Glomus jugulare erodes the jugular spine, with moth-eaten bone. Glomus tympanicum sits on the cochlear promontory. Pre-operative embolisation often uses ascending pharyngeal feeders.

q: Incomplete (open ring) enhancement opening toward the cortex suggests:
e: Demyelination enhances at the advancing edge adjacent to the white matter side.
p: Often little mass effect for its size, a T2-dark rim, and peripheral restricted diffusion. Biopsy may be needed. Abscess has a complete rim.

q: Corpus callosum body lesions with a sandwich sign on sagittal MRI in a chronic alcoholic suggest:
e: Callosal demyelination with relative sparing of the dorsal and ventral layers.
p: Associated with chronic alcoholism and malnutrition. Wernicke affects mammillary bodies. Osmotic demyelination affects the pons.

q: NF2 is characterised by bilateral:
e: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are the hallmark.
p: Also meningiomas and spinal ependymomas (MISME). NF1: optic glioma, Lisch nodules, plexiform neurofibroma, sphenoid wing dysplasia.

q: A recognised risk of balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration (BRTO) for gastric varices is:
e: Diverting flow from the gastrorenal shunt raises portal pressure and may enlarge oesophageal varices.
p: BRTO needs a gastrorenal shunt. Also ascites and hydrothorax can worsen. Complementary approach to TIPS, especially if encephalopathy is a concern.

q: The most common cause of SVC syndrome is:
e: Malignancy remains the leading cause, though benign catheter causes are rising.
p: Treat with stenting for rapid symptom relief, plus oncological treatment. Thrombotic SVC syndrome may need thrombolysis first.

q: The most common vascular complication after liver transplantation is:
e: Hepatic artery thrombosis, usually within the first month.
p: Doppler shows absent arterial flow or tardus parvus waveform. Treat urgently with thrombolysis, angioplasty or surgical revision. Biliary ischaemia follows.

q: In embolisation for bleeding duodenal ulcer, the front door/back door technique means:
o: Embolising the GDA both proximally and distally to block retrograde flow
e: Embolising only proximally allows backfilling via the pancreaticoduodenal arcade.
p: Use coils or glue. Evaluate the SMA for collateral supply. Blind embolisation is acceptable if the bleeding site is not seen.

q: Percutaneous nephrostomy access is preferably made through the:
o: Posterior calyx via the Brodel avascular line
e: The posterior lower-pole calyx along Brodel line minimises arterial injury.
p: Avoid infundibular puncture, which risks segmental arteries. Use ultrasound with fluoroscopy. Complications: bleeding, sepsis, pleural transgression with upper-pole access.

q: Thoracic duct embolisation is used for:
e: Embolising the duct via the cisterna chyli treats chyle leaks.
p: Intranodal lymphangiography with ethiodised oil (Lipiodol) opacifies the lymphatics. Success rates are good for post-operative chylothorax.

q: Unicentric Castleman disease (hyaline-vascular type) typically shows:
o: An avidly enhancing hypervascular lymph node mass
e: The hyaline-vascular type is a hypervascular, well-defined mass, often with feeding vessels.
p: Resection is curative for unicentric disease. Multicentric disease needs systemic therapy and is associated with HHV-8 and HIV.

q: An air crescent sign in a neutropenic patient who is recovering suggests:
e: Recovering neutrophils retract necrotic lung from the surrounding parenchyma.
p: The halo sign (ground-glass around a nodule) is the early sign of angioinvasive aspergillosis. Aspergilloma shows the Monod sign in a pre-existing cavity.

q: The central dot sign in Caroli disease represents:
o: Portal radicles within dilated intrahepatic ducts
e: Portal vein branches are surrounded by dilated bile ducts.
p: Caroli disease is type V choledochal cyst with ARPKD association. Complications: cholangitis, stones, cholangiocarcinoma.

q: A large encapsulated pancreatic mass with solid and cystic haemorrhagic components in a young woman is likely:
e: SPN affects young women and has a good prognosis after resection.
p: Low malignant potential. Typically in the pancreatic tail. Haemorrhagic areas give T1 hyperintensity.

q: By the Parks classification, the most common type of perianal fistula is:
e: Intersphincteric fistulas account for the largest share.
p: Use MRI to define the internal opening, relation to sphincter complex and any horseshoe tracks. St James's University Hospital classification grades 1-5 on MRI.

q: Which finding suggests transplant renal artery stenosis?
o: Tardus parvus intrarenal waveforms with high PSV at the stenosis
e: Distal tardus parvus waveform plus a high-velocity jet at the stenosis.
p: A raised resistive index is non-specific and also occurs in rejection, ATN and obstruction. Treat with angioplasty or stenting.

q: In a horseshoe kidney, the isthmus lies:
o: Anterior to the aorta and IVC, below the IMA
e: The isthmus crosses anterior to the great vessels, below the inferior mesenteric artery.
p: Associated with UPJ obstruction, stones and infection, and a higher risk of Wilms tumour. Aberrant renal arteries are common, relevant to surgery and embolisation.

q: An endometrioma typically shows on MRI:
o: T1 hyperintense (persisting on fat saturation) with T2 shading
T1 hypointense with T2 hyperintense signal
e: Chronic blood products give T1 hyperintensity and T2 shading.
p: Dermoids lose signal on fat saturation. Malignant transformation raises concern if enhancing mural nodules appear.

q: On T2 MRI, the triple sign (hypo-, iso- and hyperintense areas) is associated with:
e: Synovial sarcoma has heterogeneous signal with the triple sign; calcification occurs in about 30%.
p: Occurs near joints in young adults. Despite the name, it does not arise from synovium. Metastasises to lungs.

q: The penumbra sign on T1 MRI is associated with:
e: A T1-hyperintense rim of granulation tissue lines the abscess cavity.
p: Brodie abscess is a metaphyseal lucent lesion with a sclerotic rim and may cross the physis. Differentiate from tumour by the tract and the penumbra.

q: An Andersson lesion in ankylosing spondylitis is:
e: A destructive discovertebral lesion, often after trauma through the fused spine.
p: Romanus lesion: anterior corner erosion with sclerosis. The fused spine is brittle, so low-energy fractures occur. Imaging with CT or MRI.

q: Hyperinflated lungs with coarse patchy opacities in a post-term neonate suggest:
e: Meconium causes air-trapping with patchy atelectasis and consolidation.
p: Pneumothorax is a common complication. RDS shows low volumes with ground glass and air bronchograms. TTN shows fluid in fissures and clears in 48 to 72 hours.

q: A Meckel scan using Tc-99m pertechnetate detects:
e: Pertechnetate is taken up by gastric mucosal cells.
p: Cimetidine or pentagastrin enhance uptake. False negatives occur with small or non-gastric lesions. Meckel diverticulum: rule of 2s.

q: Doubling the distance from a point X-ray source changes radiation intensity to:
e: Inverse square law: intensity falls to a quarter.
p: Increase distance to reduce staff dose in fluoroscopy. Use lead aprons, thyroid shields and short exposures.

q: Compared with gynaecomastia, male breast cancer is more often:
o: Eccentric to the nipple, spiculated or irregular
e: Cancer is eccentric and irregular; gynaecomastia is retroareolar and often bilateral.
p: Most male breast cancers are invasive ductal. Risk factors include BRCA2 and Klinefelter syndrome.

q: Severe aortic stenosis is likely on CT calcium scoring above about:
o: 2000 AU in men and 1200 AU in women
e: Thresholds are sex-specific.
p: Useful when echo is discordant (low-flow low-gradient). Pre-TAVI CT also assesses annulus, coronary heights and access vessels.

q: A fetal MCA peak systolic velocity above what value predicts moderate-severe anaemia?
e: Above 1.5 multiples of the median.
p: Used in red cell alloimmunisation and parvovirus infection. Management includes intrauterine transfusion. The sample is taken at the proximal MCA with a near-zero angle.

q: TO-ACT evaluated endovascular thrombectomy in severe cerebral venous thrombosis and found:
o: Higher recanalisation with no safety signal
e: Thrombectomy added no benefit to standard treatment.
p: Anticoagulation remains first line even with haemorrhagic venous infarction. DOACs were comparable to warfarin in ACTION-CVT. Endovascular treatment is reserved for deterioration despite anticoagulation.

q: The spot sign on CTA in intracerebral haemorrhage predicts:
e: Contrast extravasation within the haematoma marks active bleeding.
p: Predicts expansion, poor outcome and mortality. Look for underlying vascular lesion (AVM, aneurysm, venous thrombosis) in young or atypical-location bleeds.

q: Which feature favours Rathke cleft cyst?
o: T1 hyperintense intracystic nodule without enhancement
e: The intracystic nodule is characteristic and does not enhance.
p: Located between the anterior and posterior pituitary. Craniopharyngioma enhances and usually calcifies. Most cases are asymptomatic and incidental.

q: Optic neuritis involving a long segment of the nerve and the chiasm suggests:
e: NMOSD tends to involve long posterior segments and the chiasm.
p: MS gives short anterior segment lesions. MOGAD gives long anterior involvement with perineural enhancement and often optic disc swelling.

q: Compared with chordoma, clival chondrosarcoma is more likely to be:
e: Chondrosarcoma arises off-midline from the petro-occipital synchondrosis.
p: Chordoma: midline clivus, very bright on T2 with a honeycomb pattern, bone destruction. Chondroid matrix calcification is typical of chondrosarcoma.

q: On Tc-99m brain death scintigraphy, which finding supports the diagnosis?
o: Absent intracranial perfusion with increased nasal uptake (hot nose)
e: Intracranial perfusion is absent and flow diverts to the external carotid, giving the hot nose sign.
p: Used when clinical examination or apnoea testing is unreliable. Tracer should be given as a bolus. CTA and transcranial Doppler are alternatives.

q: In pelvic congestion syndrome, ovarian vein embolisation is considered when the ovarian vein measures more than about:
e: Ovarian veins above about 6 mm with reflux and dilated parauterine veins support the diagnosis.
p: Imaging: tortuous pelvic veins over 4 mm, reflux on venography. Embolise with coils, with or without sclerosant. Exclude May-Thurner and nutcracker syndromes.

q: ULTIMA found ultrasound-facilitated catheter-directed thrombolysis, compared with heparin alone, in intermediate-risk PE:
o: Improved RV/LV ratio at 24 hours without excess major bleeding
e: RV/LV ratio improved at 24 hours.
p: The trial used low-dose lytic with ultrasound-assisted delivery. Larger trials are exploring outcomes beyond RV/LV ratio.

q: BASIL-2 in chronic limb-threatening ischaemia with infrapopliteal disease found:
o: Better amputation-free survival with vein bypass first
Better amputation-free survival with endovascular first
e: A vein-bypass-first strategy had better amputation-free survival.
p: Applies to patients with suitable vein. Endovascular therapy remains appropriate for those with high surgical risk or no vein. Decision depends on anatomy, vein quality and fitness.

q: For vessel occlusion with coils, the coil diameter is usually chosen:
e: Oversizing by about 20% anchors the coil without migrating.
p: Undersized coils migrate; oversized coils fail to pack. Detachable coils allow repositioning. Pushable coils are used in larger vessels.

q: Sclerotherapy of lymphatic malformations works best for:
e: Macrocystic lesions respond well; microcystic ones respond poorly.
p: Agents include doxycycline, OK-432 and bleomycin. Mixed lesions respond partially. Sirolimus is used for complex lesions.

q: Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon is associated with:
e: It occurs with kaposiform haemangioendothelioma or tufted angioma, not venous malformations.
p: Venous malformations are low-flow, very T2 bright and contain phleboliths; they are treated with sclerotherapy (ethanol, sodium tetradecyl sulphate, polidocanol). They can cause localised intravascular coagulopathy.

q: Perihilar ground-glass opacity with upper lobe cysts and sparing of the periphery in an immunocompromised patient suggests:
e: PJP gives diffuse perihilar ground-glass with cysts or pneumatoceles.
p: Peripheral sparing is a clue. Spontaneous pneumothorax can occur. HIV patients with CD4 under 200 are at risk.

q: A bronchogenic cyst typically appears as a:
o: Non-enhancing subcarinal or paratracheal mass of fluid or higher attenuation
e: It is a non-enhancing fluid-filled cyst, which may be dense from proteinaceous content.
p: Most common in the subcarinal or right paratracheal region. MRI is T2 bright. Air within suggests infection or communication.

q: The fallen lung sign suggests:
e: The collapsed lung falls away from the hilum toward the dependent position.
p: Persistent pneumothorax despite a chest tube and a large air leak are clues. Tracheobronchial injury is usually within 2 cm of the carina.

q: Which hepatocellular adenoma subtype shows signal drop on opposed-phase imaging?
e: HNF1A-inactivated adenomas are steatotic.
p: Inflammatory adenomas show T2 atoll sign and persistent enhancement. Beta-catenin-activated adenomas carry malignancy risk and are more common in men.

q: In the 8th edition oesophageal cancer staging, T4a refers to invasion of:
o: Pleura, pericardium, azygos vein, diaphragm or peritoneum
e: T4a invades resectable adjacent structures.
p: T4b invades unresectable structures (aorta, vertebral body, trachea). EUS is best for local T stage and nodes, PET for distant disease.

q: Comet-tail artefacts within the gallbladder wall on ultrasound suggest:
e: Cholesterol crystals in Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses create comet-tail artefacts.
p: MRCP shows the pearl necklace sign. Porcelain gallbladder shows wall calcification with shadowing.

q: Which feature is associated with renal oncocytoma but is not reliable for diagnosis?
e: A central stellate scar with spoke-wheel enhancement occurs but is also seen in RCC.
p: Imaging cannot reliably separate oncocytoma from chromophobe RCC. Management is usually surgical.

q: A fundal cleft deeper than 1 cm with two separate horns suggests:
e: Bicornuate uterus has a fundal cleft over 1 cm.
p: Septate uterus has a normal or minimally indented fundus and benefits from hysteroscopic septum resection. Arcuate uterus has a mild fundal indentation.

q: Pigmented villonodular synovitis shows blooming on GRE images because of:
e: Haemosiderin causes susceptibility blooming.
p: Monoarticular, most often the knee. T2 low-signal synovial nodules. Giant cell tumour of the tendon sheath is the localised form.

q: The Honda sign on bone scintigraphy indicates:
e: An H-shaped uptake pattern in the sacrum.
p: Vertical sacral ala fractures joined by a horizontal component. Associated with osteoporosis and radiotherapy. MRI or CT confirms.

q: Which feature favours atypical lipomatous tumour over a simple lipoma?
o: Thick septa over 2 mm and nodules
e: Thick septa and non-fatty nodules with MDM2 amplification.
p: Confirm with MDM2 testing. Deep location and size over 10 cm also raise concern. Treated with wide excision.

q: The most common craniosynostosis is:
e: Sagittal synostosis gives a long narrow head.
p: Coronal gives brachycephaly, metopic trigonocephaly. 3D CT is used for surgical planning.

q: In achondroplasia, the lumbar interpedicular distance:
e: Progressive narrowing causes spinal stenosis.
p: Other features: champagne-glass pelvis, trident hand, short ribs, small foramen magnum. Normally the distance widens caudally.

q: The ICRP threshold for lens opacity (cataract) is about:
e: The ICRP 2011 threshold is 0.5 Gy.
p: Occupational lens dose limit is 20 mSv per year averaged over five years, with no single year over 50 mSv. Interventionalists should use ceiling-suspended shields and leaded glasses.

q: On a well-positioned MLO view, the posterior nipple line length should be within what distance of the CC view?
e: The PNL on the MLO should be within about 1 cm of the CC PNL.
p: A good MLO also shows the pectoralis muscle down to the nipple level, with the inframammary fold open.

q: Compared with omphalocele, gastroschisis is:
o: Right paraumbilical, uncovered and usually isolated
e: Gastroschisis is a right paraumbilical defect with free-floating bowel and no covering.
p: Omphalocele is midline, covered by membrane and associated with aneuploidy and other anomalies. Raised AFP in both.

q: The ACR elective premedication regimen for prior moderate-severe contrast reaction includes prednisone:
o: 50 mg orally at 13, 7 and 1 hours, plus diphenhydramine 50 mg at 1 hour
e: Prednisone 50 mg at 13, 7 and 1 hours, plus diphenhydramine 50 mg 1 hour before.
p: An accelerated regimen with IV methylprednisolone or hydrocortisone is used when needed. Premedication reduces but does not eliminate reactions.
